title: How to Save Money on Pizza Delivery: 11 Tactics
excerpt: Most advice about saving money on pizza is either obvious or wrong. Here are the eleven things that move the total, ranked by how much they save.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: A woman at home smiling at her phone beside an open pizza box

pricing.label: Family order, two ways
pricing.note: Two large pizzas, a side and a drink: delivered at menu price with fee and tip, versus two $7.99 carryout pizzas and Bread Bites with the drink bought elsewhere. Worked from prices checked at one store.

faqs.question: What is the single biggest saving on a pizza order?
faqs.answer: Switching from delivery to carryout, if collecting is practical for you. It removes the delivery fee, the tip and usually unlocks a lower flat price on the pizza itself, which together is roughly thirteen to eighteen dollars on a large 1-topping pizza.

faqs.question: Do coupon codes still work at pizza chains?
faqs.answer: Increasingly the discounts are built into the site as deal tiles rather than typed codes. Both routes exist, but the deal tiles are where most of the value now sits; you open the deal and build your order inside it, and the cart shows whether your basket qualifies.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to order two mediums or one large?
faqs.answer: One large is almost always more pizza per dollar than one medium, but two mediums under a flat-rate bundle can beat one large at menu price. The rule that holds is to compare price per square inch rather than price per pizza.

content:
There is a lot of advice about saving money on takeout pizza and most of it is worth nothing. Telling someone to look for coupons is not advice; it is a description of wanting to spend less. What follows is the list, in the order of how much money each one saves on a typical order.

For context: using menu prices checked at a Domino’s in Columbus, Ohio, a family order of two large pizzas, a side and a drink comes to about fifty-three dollars delivered at menu price with a fee and tip — and about twenty-two dollars picked up on the $7.99 carryout deal, with the drink bought elsewhere. That thirty-dollar spread is the whole subject of this article. Nothing here involves eating less pizza.

1. Switch to carryout, when it is practical

This is the largest single saving available and it is not close. Picking up your own order removes the delivery fee, removes the tip, and — this is the part people miss — usually unlocks a separate, cheaper price on the pizza itself. Chains run flat-rate carryout offers that simply do not exist in delivery mode.

Add those three together on a large 1-topping pizza and you are looking at roughly thirteen to eighteen dollars — more than the $7.99 the pizza costs on the carryout deal. The caveat is real, though: if collecting means a twenty-minute drive each way, you have spent forty minutes and a gallon of gas, which eats a large part of the saving. Carryout wins when the store is close.

2. Price your basket both ways before you check out

Domino’s runs two parallel pricing systems: menu prices, and deal prices. They are not the same items at different discounts — they are separate structures, and which one wins depends on what you are ordering.

Mix & Match prices every item at $6.99, which is a saving on an $8.99 sandwich but a loss on 16 Bread Bites that cost $5.99 on the menu. The Perfect Combo at $19.99 only beats the menu if you actually want both mediums, the Bread Bites and the twists. The only way to know is to price the basket both ways, which takes ninety seconds.

3. Order the most expensive thing inside a flat-price deal

Mix & Match charges the same $6.99 for every qualifying item, so the saving depends entirely on what you put in it. At the store we checked, an oven-baked sandwich ($8.99) saves $2.00, a pasta ($8.49) saves $1.50, and 16 Bread Bites ($5.99) cost you a dollar more than ordering them off the menu. The $7.99 carryout deal works the same way: a large 1-topping pizza (about $15.49 at our estimated menu price) saves more than an 8-piece wings ($10.99).

This sounds obvious written down. In practice, people default to ordering what they normally order and then apply whatever deal fits, rather than choosing the item that extracts the most from the deal. Reverse the order of those decisions.

4. Take the drinks off the order

Soft drinks from a pizza store cost up to twice supermarket price — a 2-liter was $4.49 in our check. A two-liter bottle and a couple of individual drinks on a family order is five or six dollars of pure convenience charge, and it is the least painful thing on the list to remove because you are not giving up any food.

The exception is a deal on your store page that includes a drink. If one does, take it.

5. Count your toppings before you check out

Build-your-own pizzas start cheap and get expensive fast, because each topping carries a charge that scales with pizza size. At our estimated $1.50 per topping on a large, four toppings take a $13.99 large cheese to $19.99 — the same as a large specialty pizza, which carries six to eight toppings. From the fourth topping on, check whether a specialty pizza already has what you want.

Almost nobody checks this at the point of ordering. It is worth thirty seconds of comparison every time.

6. Use the free modifications

Light sauce, extra sauce, light cheese, well-done bake, square cut instead of wedge cut — these are usually free in the online pizza builder, which shows a price if one applies. Extra cheese and extra toppings are the paid ones. Knowing which is which means you can customize substantially without touching the price.

7. Sign in before you order, every time

Loyalty points are not earned on guest checkouts, so sign in before you pay. Every guest order is a small amount of free pizza given up.

Worth knowing: at most chains, carryout orders earn points at the same rate as delivery. People assume they do not and lose points on exactly the orders they should be placing.

8. Order early rather than at peak

This does not change the price directly, but it changes what you get for it. Placing an order at 6:30pm on a Friday puts you into the deepest part of the queue at every store in the country. The same order at 5:15pm arrives faster and in better condition, and you have paid the same money for a materially better product.

9. Scale up rather than adding items

Going from a medium to a large costs a few dollars and adds about a third more pizza. Adding a second medium costs the full price of a second pizza. When feeding more people, the first move is always to increase size, not quantity.

10. Stop paying for wings as a main course

Wings are the worst food-per-dollar item on a pizza menu because a large share of the weight is bone. As a side for a table, fine. As the thing that feeds a person, a second pizza costs less and feeds more.

11. Tip on the driver, not on the total

This one is not about spending less — it is about spending it in the right place. The delivery fee is a store charge and, at most chains, does not reach the driver. Cutting the tip because a fee was already applied is a misunderstanding that costs the person who drove to your house.

If your budget is tight, cut the drinks and the extra cheese. Do not cut the tip.

Putting it together

The tactics stack. On the family order worked out at the top of this article, using carryout where practical, dropping the drinks, choosing the deal that suits the basket and putting the highest-priced items into it takes a fifty-dollar order to the low twenties without removing a single slice of pizza from the table.

None of it requires waiting for a special promotion or hunting for a code. It requires ordering deliberately rather than by habit, which is the only pizza-saving advice we would stand behind.

title: Carryout vs Delivery: The Real Cost Difference, Worked Out
excerpt: Everyone knows carryout is cheaper. Almost nobody knows by how much, or at what driving distance the saving stops being worth it. We did the arithmetic.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: Side by side: a customer collecting a pizza box at a counter, and a pizza handed over at a front door

pricing.label: Same large pizza, both ways
pricing.note: A large 1-topping pizza on the $7.99 carryout deal versus the same pizza delivered at menu price (about $15.49) with a $3–6 fee and a $3–5 tip.

faqs.question: How much cheaper is carryout than delivery?
faqs.answer: On a single large 1-topping pizza, roughly thirteen to eighteen dollars: the $7.99 carryout deal against about $15.49 at menu price, plus a delivery fee of three to six dollars and a three-to-five-dollar tip. On a large multi-item order the gap narrows in percentage terms because the fee and tip are spread across more food.

faqs.question: Does the delivery fee go to the driver?
faqs.answer: Not at Domino’s: the company says its delivery charge is not a tip, and each store sets its own. Drivers are paid a wage plus tips, which is why cutting the tip because a fee was charged hurts the driver rather than the store.

faqs.question: At what distance does carryout stop being worth it?
faqs.answer: Roughly at the point where the round trip passes thirty minutes of driving. Beyond that, fuel and time consume the saving on a single-pizza order, though it can still make sense on a large one.

content:
Carryout is cheaper than delivery. That is not in dispute and it is not interesting. The useful questions are how much cheaper, why the gap is that size, and at what point driving to pick up your own pizza stops making financial sense.

Where the gap actually comes from

People assume the difference is the delivery fee. The fee is the smallest of three components.

Component one: the fee itself

Typically three to six dollars, set by each store rather than by how far away you are. It is a store charge, not a driver payment — more on that below.

Component two: the tip

A standard tip on a single-pizza order is three to five dollars, and on a larger order proportionally more. This is a real cost of having food delivered even though it is technically discretionary.

Component three: the price of the pizza

This is the one people miss, and it is the largest. Domino’s $7.99 carryout deal covers a large 1-topping pizza that costs about $15.49 on the menu (our estimate; a large cheese pizza was $13.99 at the store we checked). The deal does not exist in delivery mode, so the same pizza delivered is charged at menu price.

Stack all three and a large 1-topping pizza that costs $7.99 picked up comes to roughly $21 to $26 delivered. That is not a markup on delivery; it is three separate charges pointing in the same direction.

Why the pizza itself is priced differently

A carryout order costs the store almost nothing to fulfil beyond the food. Nobody drives anywhere, no vehicle is insured, no time is spent out of the building. A delivery order consumes fifteen to thirty minutes of a driver's shift.

Chains would rather you collected, and they price accordingly. The flat carryout rate is a discount to change your behavior, not a reward for loyalty.

When delivery is the right call anyway

The saving is real, but it is not free. Here is when I would still pay it.

  • The store is more than fifteen minutes away. A thirty-minute round trip costs fuel and half an hour of your evening, which is a real price even against a thirteen-dollar saving.
  • You are ordering a lot. On a fifty-dollar order the fee and tip are a smaller share of the total, and the flat carryout rate usually applies to one pizza rather than four.
  • Weather, or no car. In a Chicago February the calculation changes completely, and it should.
  • The food is temperature-sensitive. A lava cake or cheesy bread collected and eaten in ten minutes is better than the same item delivered. But a pizza in your own car for twenty minutes is not better than a pizza in an insulated bag for twenty-five.

The distance where it flips

Working from a saving of about thirteen dollars on a single large pizza and rough vehicle running costs, the break-even lands somewhere around a thirty-minute round trip — and that is before you value your own time at anything.

Value your time at even ten dollars an hour and a twenty-minute round trip has consumed a quarter of the saving before you have paid for gas. For a single pizza from a store fifteen minutes away, delivery is defensible. For a single pizza from a store four minutes away, carryout is close to free money.

The fee and the tip are not the same thing

This is the part I will not be neutral about.

At most chains the delivery fee does not go to the driver. It goes to the store and helps cover what offering delivery costs it. Drivers are typically paid a wage plus their tips, and drivers who use their own car usually get a mileage reimbursement that is separate from the fee.

What that means practically: when someone sees a five-dollar delivery fee and reduces their tip because they feel they have already paid for delivery, the person absorbing that is the driver, not the chain. It is one of the most common misunderstandings in the whole business, and it is expensive for the people least able to absorb it.

If you want to spend less on a delivery order, cut the drinks, cut the extra cheese, order a bundle instead of menu items. There are half a dozen levers before you get to the tip.

Practical rules

  • Choose carryout or delivery before you build the basket. Carryout-only pricing does not appear if the site has you in delivery mode.
  • If you are collecting, use every topping the flat-rate offer covers, and check what each extra one adds.
  • If you are having it delivered, order in a way that spreads the fee across more food — one larger order beats two small ones.
  • Do not drive fifteen minutes each way for one pizza unless you wanted the drive anyway — fuel and time eat most of the saving.

The short version

Carryout saves roughly thirteen to eighteen dollars on a single large 1-topping pizza — the deal price, the fee and the tip together — and less, proportionally, on a big order. It is worth doing when the store is close and not worth doing when it is not. And the delivery fee is not the tip, whatever the checkout screen implies by putting them next to each other.

title: The Best Domino’s Deals Right Now, Ranked by What They Save
excerpt: The four Domino’s US deals we could confirm in November 2026, ranked by what each saves against menu prices checked at a real store.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Four friends at a restaurant table with four pizzas, one checking a phone

faqs.question: What is the best Domino’s deal right now?
faqs.answer: For one or two people who can pick up, the $7.99 carryout deal on a large 1-topping pizza — at least $6.00 (43%) off the $13.99 menu price of a large cheese pizza at the store we checked. For three or four people, the $19.99 Perfect Combo is the cheapest per head.

faqs.question: Which Domino’s deal works for delivery?
faqs.answer: Mix & Match ($6.99 each for two or more items) is reported to work for delivery as well as carryout. The $7.99 deal is carryout only. Delivery adds a fee and a tip that no deal covers.

faqs.question: What should I pick on Mix & Match?
faqs.answer: The dearest items you will eat. A medium 2-topping pizza (about $14.99 at menu price by our estimate) saves about $8.00 in a $6.99 slot; 16 Bread Bites already cost $5.99, so they are cheaper outside the deal.

faqs.question: Does Domino’s have a family deal?
faqs.answer: The closest is the $19.99 Perfect Combo: two medium 1-topping pizzas, 16 Parmesan Bread Bites and 8 Cinnamon Twists. For a bigger group, several large pizzas on the $7.99 carryout deal give the most pizza for the money if someone can pick up.

content:
Quick answer

For one or two people who can pick up, the $7.99 carryout deal saves the most — at least $6.00 (43%) on a large pizza. For three or four people, the $19.99 Perfect Combo is the cheapest per head. If you need delivery, use Mix & Match and put the dearest items in it.

Deal prices are as reported in November 2026 from Domino’s deals page wording and two deal roundups; we have not tested them at checkout. Menu prices were checked at a Domino’s in Columbus, Ohio, on October 25, 2026, before tax. Your store may differ.

Most “best deals” lists name every offer they can find. This one is shorter on purpose: these are the Domino’s US deals we could confirm, ranked by what each one actually takes off the same food at menu price. Promotions rotate, so the last section shows how to check your own store in under a minute.

1. Carryout deal — $7.99

What you get: a large 1-topping pizza, or an 8-piece order of wings or boneless chicken, among the reported choices. Carryout only, at participating stores, and some charge more. Domino’s fine print says you may need to ask for it.

What it saves: a large hand-tossed cheese pizza was $13.99 at the store we checked, so the deal takes off at least $6.00 — 43% — before you count the topping it includes. On a large pepperoni (about $15.49 by our estimate) the gap is about $7.50. On 8 wings ($10.99) it saves only $3.00, so put the pizza on the deal rather than the wings.

Best for: one to three people with a store close enough to pick up. Skipping delivery also removes the delivery fee and the tip, which no other deal does.

2. Perfect Combo — $19.99

What you get: two medium 1-topping pizzas, 16-piece Parmesan Bread Bites and an 8-piece order of Cinnamon Twists. Sources differ on whether a 2-liter drink is included, so check the tile.

What it saves: two medium cheese pizzas (about $11.99 each by our estimate) and the Bread Bites ($5.99, checked) come to about $29.97 before the toppings and the twists. So the combo saves about $10 — and the real figure is higher because we have not priced the twists or the toppings.

Best for: three or four people. At $19.99 for four, it is about $5.00 a head, the lowest of any deal here.

3. Mix & Match — $6.99 each

What you get: two or more items from a qualifying list at $6.99 each — a medium 2-topping pizza, pasta, an oven-baked sandwich, Stuffed Cheesy Bread and more. Reported to work for delivery as well as carryout; some locations charge more.

What it saves: it depends entirely on what you pick.

ItemMenu priceSaved at $6.99
Medium 2-topping pizzaabout $14.99 (est.)about $8.00
Italian sandwich$8.99$2.00
Stuffed Cheesy Bread$8.49$1.50
Chicken Alfredo Pasta$8.49$1.50
16 Bread Bites$5.99none — $1.00 dearer on the deal

Best for: two people who want different things, and anyone who needs delivery. The medium 2-topping pizza is the slot that earns the most; Bread Bites are cheaper bought outside the deal. Our Mix & Match guide works through more combinations.

4. Domino’s Rewards — a free medium pizza

What you get: 10 points for each signed-in order of $5 or more; 60 points buy a free medium 2-topping pizza, with smaller rewards at lower totals.

What it saves: a medium 2-topping pizza is about $14.99 at menu price by our estimate, earned over six orders — roughly $2.50 back per order. Not dramatic, but it costs nothing except signing in, carryout included.

Best for: anyone who orders every few weeks. Whether a reward can go into the same order as a deal depends on the current terms, so check in the app. More on how the points work.

Which deal for which order

  • One person, can pick up: the $7.99 carryout large. Leftovers are lunch.
  • Two people, different tastes: two Mix & Match items — a medium 2-topping pizza and a sandwich — for $13.98.
  • Three or four people: the $19.99 Perfect Combo.
  • Six to ten people, someone can drive: several large pizzas on the carryout deal — four are about $32.
  • Six to ten people, delivered: two Perfect Combos, or Mix & Match pizzas if the group wants more choice.

What is not a deal

A time of day. We found no Domino’s happy hour or late-night discount in the US; the prices above apply whenever the store is open. See our happy hour research.

Codes from coupon sites. Most are expired or tied to someone else’s account. Domino’s deals are mostly tiles that apply in the basket, not codes. Why codes fail.

A bigger order to reach a threshold. Spending eight extra dollars to unlock a five-dollar saving is not a saving, however the screen presents it.

How to check your own store in a minute

  1. Enter your address on the official app or dominos.com, so you see the store that will make your order.
  2. Switch to carryout first and open Deals — carryout-only prices do not show in delivery mode.
  3. Check the deal prices against this page. If yours are higher, your store has set its own price.
  4. Build the basket once on the deal and once at menu price, and keep the cheaper total.

If your store’s prices differ from ours, tell us — real prices from readers are the most useful thing you can send.

title: Pizza Coupon Codes Explained: Why Yours Did Not Work
excerpt: Codes fail for four predictable reasons. Understanding how chain promotion systems are built explains all of them, and prevents most.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Close-up of friends laughing while one looks at a pizza ordering app on her phone

faqs.question: Why does my pizza coupon code say invalid?
faqs.answer: The four common causes are that your store is not participating, your basket does not meet the qualifying item requirements, the offer has expired, or you are in delivery mode for a carryout-only offer. Store participation is the one people check last and it is the most frequent culprit.

faqs.question: Are typed coupon codes being phased out?
faqs.answer: Largely replaced by deal tiles on the store deals page, which you open and build your order inside. Codes still exist for targeted and partnership promotions, but the everyday discounts have moved into the ordering interface itself.

faqs.question: Where do the codes on coupon aggregator sites come from?
faqs.answer: Mostly from expired national promotions and targeted offers that were never meant to be public. Hit rates on those sites are low, which is why checking your own store's deals page is a better use of thirty seconds.

content:
At Domino’s

In November 2026 we could confirm four US Domino’s deals: the $7.99 carryout deal, Mix & Match at $6.99 an item, the $19.99 Perfect Combo and Domino’s Rewards. We found no current percentage-off code we could stand behind, so we do not list any.

Each store chooses which offers it runs, so they appear on your store’s deals page once you enter an address. Details and worked savings are on our deals page.

A coupon code is a key. Your basket is a lock. When the key does not turn, it is usually because the lock is a different shape than you assumed — and the shape is set at store level, which is the part nobody explains.

How chain promotion systems actually work

National chains are mostly franchise networks. Head office designs promotions and sets the terms; individual franchisees decide whether to participate, because they absorb the margin cost of the discount in their own store.

That single fact explains most coupon failures. A promotion advertised nationally is not automatically live at your store. It is live at stores that opted in. The ad is national; the offer is local.

Layered on top of that is the ordering system, which validates a code against three things: whether this store participates, whether your basket contains the qualifying items, and whether the offer is inside its date and time window. Fail any one and you get the same unhelpful message.

The four reasons codes fail

1. Your store is not participating

The most common cause and the least visible. There is no way to tell from the ad. The practical test is to look at your own store's deals page after entering your address — if the offer is not listed there, your store is not running it, and no amount of retyping will change that.

2. Your basket does not qualify

Offers specify qualifying items with more precision than the headline suggests. A two-item bundle may require two medium pizzas, not any two items. A percentage discount may exclude items already on promotion.

The tell here is that the code is accepted but the discount is smaller than expected, or the code is rejected with a message about eligible items. Swap one item and try again.

3. The offer has expired

Codes circulate on aggregator sites long after they stop working. Many of the codes you find by searching are old offers that were never taken down.

4. You are in the wrong order mode

Carryout-only offers do not appear or apply while the site has you in delivery mode, and vice versa. This catches people trying to use a carryout deal while still in delivery mode.

Set the order type first, before you build the basket. Switching afterwards can re-price the basket or clear it.

Why codes are disappearing

Chains have largely moved from typed codes to deal tiles — a list of current offers for your store, which you open and build your order inside.

From the chain's perspective this is better in every way: no expired codes leaking value, no aggregator sites distributing offers to people who would have paid full price, and complete control over what each store shows. From your perspective it is also better, because the offers you see are the ones your store is running.

Codes still exist for targeted promotions, email campaigns and partnership offers. But if you are hunting for a code on a search engine, you are looking in the place where the value has already left.

Where the discounts actually are now

  • Your store's deals page. Enter your address first, then look. What is listed there is what your store is running.
  • The chain's own app. Some offers appear only in the app, so check its deals page as well as the website’s.
  • Email and account notifications. Offers sent to your account are made for you, so they are worth checking before you order.
  • Loyalty points. The most reliable discount of all, because it does not depend on any promotion running.

A sensible troubleshooting order

  1. Confirm your delivery or carryout mode matches the offer.
  2. Check the offer appears on your own store's deals page.
  3. Read the qualifying item list and compare it to your basket, item by item.
  4. Check the date and any time-of-day restriction.
  5. If all four pass and it still fails, call the store and ask; they can tell you what they are running.

What to stop doing

Stop searching for codes on aggregator sites. The hit rate is low, the codes are mostly expired, and the thirty seconds is better spent looking at the deals page for your actual store, where the listed offers are the ones it is actually running.

The discount did not disappear. It moved into the ordering interface, which is a better place for it to be.

A note on why this changed so fast

Ten years ago, a printed coupon on the back of a supermarket receipt was a perfectly good distribution channel for a pizza discount. It was slow, it was untargeted, and crucially it was hard to leak — one coupon reached one household and expired on paper.

Digital codes broke that. A code intended for a few thousand lapsed customers gets posted publicly within hours and is then redeemed by people who were going to order anyway. From the chain's point of view that is not a discount, it is a straight margin loss, and the industry response was entirely predictable: move the offer into an interface the chain controls.

Which is why the deals page personalized to your store is now where the value sits, and why the codes floating around search results are almost uniformly dead. The offer did not get worse. It moved somewhere the chain can meter it.

What to do when nothing is running

Some weeks your store has nothing good on. It happens, particularly at smaller franchise operations in quiet trading periods. The reliable fallbacks, in order:

  • Switch to carryout. The flat carryout rate is close to a permanent fixture at most chains and rarely disappears entirely.
  • Check a second store if more than one serves your address. Participation is decided individually, so a neighboring store may be running something yours is not.
  • Look at your points balance. A redemption does not depend on any promotion running at all, which makes it the one discount that is always available once you have earned it.
  • Shift the order to a weekday lunchtime if timing is flexible. Off-peak offers exist precisely because those hours are quiet.

None of that requires a code, which is rather the point.

title: Hand Tossed vs Thin Crust vs Pan: Which to Order?
excerpt: Switching between hand tossed and thin crust is free — and it changes the texture, calories, topping capacity and whether leftovers are worth keeping.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A vegetable pizza on a table next to a closed pizza box and a phone

faqs.question: Which pizza crust has the fewest calories?
faqs.answer: Thin crust — on a large, about 210 calories a slice for cheese against 290 for hand tossed, with toppings unchanged. Because crust choice is usually free, it is the cheapest calorie reduction available on a chain pizza.

faqs.question: Does pan pizza cost more?
faqs.answer: Usually a small upcharge over hand tossed — about $1.50 on a medium by our estimate — and it can apply on top of deal pricing rather than being absorbed into it. At Domino’s the Handmade Pan is sold as a medium only.

faqs.question: Which crust holds the most toppings?
faqs.answer: Pan, then hand tossed, then thin. A thin crust struggles beyond two or three toppings, particularly wet vegetables, because there is not enough structure to support the weight and moisture.

content:
Crust is the most consequential decision on a pizza order, and part of it is free. Changing from hand tossed to thin crust costs nothing and changes the calorie count, the texture, the number of toppings the pizza can carry and how it survives until tomorrow.

Here is what each one actually is, and when to pick it.

Hand tossed: the default

A medium-thickness base with a raised outer rim, soft in the middle, chewy at the edge. This is the crust every deal assumes and every price is quoted against.

Best for: most orders. It carries three or four toppings comfortably, it survives a delivery journey, and it reheats acceptably. There is a reason it is the default.

Weaknesses: it is a compromise. It is not as crisp as thin, not as rich as pan, and it does nothing exceptionally.

Calories: 290 per slice of a large cheese pizza, as listed in the official cart.

Thin crust: the calorie decision

Rolled rather than tossed, no raised rim, crisp rather than chewy, usually cut into squares.

Best for: anyone who wants to cut calories without changing what they eat. On a large it is roughly 80 calories a slice lighter than hand tossed (about 210 against 290), with the cheese and toppings identical, and it costs nothing to switch. As a nutrition intervention this is unusually painless — nothing is removed from the pizza except dough.

Also better for anyone who dislikes the doughy center of a chain pizza, which is a real and common complaint.

Weaknesses: it will not hold heavy toppings. Two or three is the practical limit and wet vegetables need a well-done bake. It also feeds fewer people than the same-diameter hand tossed, because there is less food, and it goes stale fastest of the three.

Calories: about 210 per slice of a large cheese pizza — our estimate from published nutrition data.

Pan: the rich one

Baked in an oiled pan, which fries the underside as it bakes and produces a thick, golden, slightly crunchy bottom edge.

Best for: people who want the crust to be part of the meal rather than a vehicle. Also the best of the three for leftovers by some distance — the oil in the base keeps it from drying out overnight, and a reheated pan slice in a hot oven is good.

Weaknesses: it usually carries an upcharge, that upcharge is often applied on top of deal pricing, and at Domino’s the Handmade Pan comes in a medium only, so it is not an option when you want a large. It is also the heaviest crust for its size.

Calories: about 280 per slice of a medium cheese pizza cut into eight — our estimate. A medium slice is smaller than a large one, so that is a lot for the size.

Domino’s other crusts

Hand tossed, thin and pan are the three this guide compares, but the Domino’s cart offers more:

  • New York Style — thinner and foldable, and the only crust that comes as a 16-inch extra large. If you want the biggest pizza for the money, this is the crust you get.
  • Gluten Free — a 10-inch small only, made in the same kitchen as everything else, so Domino’s does not recommend it for celiac disease. Our gluten-free guide covers what that means.
  • Parmesan Stuffed Crust — listed in the cart we checked; we did not record its price, so check the upcharge before you choose it.

The comparison in practice

Take the same pizza with pepperoni and mushroom, and change nothing but the crust (pan as a medium, since that is the only size it comes in):

  • Thin: the lightest option, cut into squares, best kept to two or three toppings.
  • Hand tossed: the default, takes any topping load, no crust upcharge.
  • Pan: the thickest, medium only, the most calories, and it can carry a crust upcharge.

Over a whole large pizza, choosing thin instead of hand tossed saves roughly 640 calories, from a decision that takes one click and costs nothing.

How to choose, quickly

Ordering for a group? Hand tossed. It is the default crust, comes in every size and takes any number of toppings.

Watching calories? Thin crust. It is the largest free reduction available on a chain pizza and does not touch the toppings.

Ordering four or five toppings? Pan or hand tossed. Thin is best kept to two or three.

Using a deal? Hand tossed or thin, since pan may carry an upcharge that eats into the discount.

Free modifications worth knowing

Whatever crust you pick, these are usually free in the online pizza builder, which shows a price if one applies:

  • Well done. Extra oven time. It can help with a soft center on a vegetable-heavy pizza and gives a thin crust more crispness. It may not suit a barbecue-sauce base, where the sugar can catch.
  • Light sauce. Can help if you find a thin crust goes soft.
  • Light cheese. A real calorie reduction.
  • Square cut. Offered on more than just thin crust in the online builder. Handy for sharing at a table where people are grazing.

The short answer

Hand tossed if you have no strong preference. Thin crust if calories matter, because it is the only free lever of that size. Pan if you want the crust to be the point, and if you are prepared for the upcharge.

The one thing not worth doing is defaulting without thinking about it. Between hand tossed and thin it is free, reversible next time, and changes the pizza more than any single topping.

What crust does to the rest of your order

Crust choice quietly changes decisions further down the basket, and it is worth thinking one step ahead.

A large thin crust has less food on it than a large hand tossed of the same diameter, so a table that would be satisfied by one hand-tossed large may want a side alongside a thin one. That side costs money the free crust switch did not. Ordering thin crust to save calories and then adding cheesy bread to fill the gap is a net loss on both counts.

Pan works the other way. It is more filling per slice, so a pan pizza often removes the need for a side entirely — which can offset the upcharge that made it look expensive in the first place.

A practical ordering script

If you want a single default that will rarely be wrong: hand tossed, well done, one meat topping and as many vegetables as you like. That combination survives delivery, holds its toppings, suits a mixed table, is priced at the standard rate inside every deal, and lands in the middle of the calorie range without anyone having to think about it.

Deviate from that deliberately — thin when calories are the priority, pan when you want leftovers or when the crust is the point. What is not worth doing is deviating by accident, which is what happens when you click through the default without noticing there was a choice at all.

title: Large vs Medium Pizza: The Math Nobody Does at Checkout
excerpt: A large pizza is not a slightly bigger medium. It is about a third more pizza, and it costs well under a third more.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Two pizzas of different sizes side by side on wooden boards
keywords: how many people does a large pizza feed

pricing.label: Cheese pizza, medium to extra large
pricing.note: Rounded from the prices on this site: the large checked at a Columbus, Ohio store, the other sizes our estimates. The area increases faster than the price does at every step.

faqs.question: Is a large pizza better value than a medium?
faqs.answer: Almost always. A fourteen-inch large has about 36% more area than a twelve-inch medium but, on the prices on this site, costs about 17% more ($13.99 against about $11.99), which makes the price per square inch meaningfully lower.

faqs.question: Are two mediums better than one large?
faqs.answer: Two twelve-inch mediums give more total area than one fourteen-inch large, so if a deal prices two mediums near the price of one large, the mediums win on quantity. At standard menu prices, one large wins on price per square inch.

faqs.question: How many people does a large pizza feed?
faqs.answer: Two to three adults as a meal, or four with sides on the table. A large cut into eight slices gives three people two to three slices each, which is where most people naturally stop.

content:
Pizza is sold by diameter and eaten by area, and those two things do not scale together. That single mismatch is responsible for most of the money people leave on the table when they order.

A twelve-inch medium has about 113 square inches of pizza. A fourteen-inch large has about 154. That is about 36% more food for two extra inches of width — and on the prices on this site, that 36% more food costs about seventeen percent more money.

The size ladder, worked through

Using the cheese pizza prices on this site — the large checked at a Columbus, Ohio store on 25 October 2026, the other sizes our estimates:

SizeDiameterApprox. areaPricePrice per sq inch
Small10 in79 sq in$8.99 (est.)11.4¢
Medium12 in113 sq in$11.99 (est.)10.6¢
Large14 in154 sq in$13.99 (checked)9.1¢
Extra Large (New York Style)16 in201 sq in$16.99 (est.)8.5¢

The pattern is consistent and it goes one way: every step up the ladder lowers the price per square inch. Going from small to extra-large cuts the unit cost of pizza by about a quarter.

The small is, by this measure, the worst-value pizza size. It exists for people ordering alone who do not want leftovers, which is a legitimate reason to buy it — but it is not a cheap pizza, it is a small one.

Where the intuition goes wrong

People compare pizzas by diameter because that is the number on the menu. Two inches sounds like a small difference. But area scales with the square of the radius, so two inches of diameter on a twelve-inch pizza is a much bigger jump than the number implies.

Put concretely: few people would describe a large as a third more pizza than a medium, but that is what it is.

The two-mediums question

This comes up constantly, usually because a deal prices two mediums attractively.

Two twelve-inch mediums give 226 square inches. One fourteen-inch large gives 154. So two mediums are nearly fifty percent more pizza than one large — meaningfully more food, and if a bundle prices them close to a single large, the mediums are clearly the better buy.

At standard menu prices, though, two mediums cost far more than one large while a single large costs less per square inch. The deal is what flips it, not the sizes themselves.

The useful rule: if you need more pizza, size up first and add a second pizza only when you have run out of sizes. Going medium to large costs a few dollars; adding a second medium costs a whole pizza.

When a smaller pizza is the right answer

Value per square inch is not the only consideration.

  • Two people with different tastes. Two smalls with different toppings can beat one large that half the table only tolerates. A half-and-half large is another option; check in the cart what the second half adds.
  • Pan crust. Domino’s Handmade Pan comes in medium only, so there is no ladder to climb.
  • Thin crust. There is less food on the same diameter, so a large thin crust feeds fewer people than a large hand tossed. Size up accordingly.
  • You will not eat it. Cheap pizza in the bin is not cheap. Thin crust in particular is poor the next day.

How much does each size actually feed?

Working from typical appetites rather than official portion guidance:

  • Small (10 in): one adult, comfortably.
  • Medium (12 in): two adults, or one with leftovers.
  • Large (14 in): two to three adults, or four with sides on the table.
  • Extra-large (16 in): three to four adults, or five with sides.

The planning number used across this site is two slices per adult when there are sides, three when the pizza is the whole meal — more for big appetites.

What to do with this

Three practical takeaways.

Size up before you add. The step up the ladder is always cheaper per unit of pizza than a whole additional pizza.

Work out your store's price per square inch once. The absolute prices move; the ratios stay stable. One calculation tells you where the value sits for years.

Ignore the diameter, think about the area. Two inches is not a small difference. It is the difference between feeding two people and feeding three.

Why chains price it this way

It is tempting to read the size ladder as generosity. It is not — it is cost structure.

The expensive parts of making a pizza barely change with size. Someone still takes the order, stretches a base, applies sauce and cheese, runs it through an oven and boxes it. The additional cost of a fourteen-inch pizza over a twelve-inch one is a modest amount of dough, sauce, cheese and a marginally larger box.

So the store can charge seventeen percent more for 36% more pizza and still do well on the sale. Sizing up is a rare case where what is good for you and what is good for the store point the same direction.

The one place the math stops working

Everything above assumes you eat the pizza. Cheap pizza in the bin is not cheap, and the calculation reverses completely on any pizza that reheats badly.

Thin crust is the clearest case: it stales fastest of any base and a large thin crust bought for a household of two is often a large thin crust with a third of it wasted. Pan is the opposite — it is good the next day, so sizing up carries less risk.

The honest rule is to size up to the largest pizza your household will finish across two sittings, and to weight that judgment by which crust you have chosen. That is a slightly less satisfying answer than always order the extra-large, but it is the one that survives contact with a real fridge.

title: How to Order Pizza Online Without Overpaying
excerpt: The order in which you click things changes what you pay. Here is the sequence that gets you the lowest total.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A woman in her kitchen holding up a phone showing a pizza menu, with a pizza box on the counter

faqs.question: Should I choose delivery or carryout first?
faqs.answer: First, before anything else. Carryout-only pricing does not appear while the site has you in delivery mode, and switching later re-prices the basket or clears it entirely at some chains.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to order on the app than the website?
faqs.answer: Menu prices are generally the same, but some offers appear only in the app. Check the deals page in both before a large order.

faqs.question: Should I order through a third-party delivery app?
faqs.answer: Generally not, if the chain delivers to you directly. Aggregator platforms typically carry marked-up menu prices plus their own service fees, and orders placed through them usually do not earn chain loyalty points.

content:
Two people can order the same large 1-topping pizza from the same Domino’s on the same evening and pay $7.99 or around $21–26. The pizza is identical. What differs is the sequence of decisions: carryout or delivery, and whether the order went through the deal.

Here is the sequence that works, with the reasoning for each step.

Step 1: Choose the chain's own channel

Order from the chain's site or app, not a third-party delivery platform, if the chain delivers to your address directly.

Aggregator platforms typically list marked-up menu prices, add their own service fees, and — importantly — orders placed through them usually do not earn chain loyalty points. On a thirty-dollar order the combined difference can easily be several dollars.

Between the website and the app, prices are generally the same, but some offers appear only in the app. If you order often, it is worth checking both deal pages.

Step 2: Set the order type before anything else

Delivery or carryout, chosen first.

This matters more than it sounds. Carryout-only offers do not display while the site has you in delivery mode. If you build a basket in delivery mode and switch afterwards, some chains re-price everything and others clear the basket entirely.

Step 3: Enter your address and confirm your store

Store assignment determines which offers you see, because franchisees opt into promotions individually. Two stores four miles apart can show different deals.

If more than one store serves your address, it is worth checking both. This is uncommon in dense cities and quite common in suburban areas.

Step 4: Sign in before you build the basket

Points do not attach to guest orders. Signing in halfway through checkout occasionally clears the basket and sometimes loses an applied offer.

Sign in first, every time. It takes ten seconds and it is an easy step to skip.

Step 5: Read the deals page before the menu

This is the step that separates a cheap order from an expensive one.

Look at the current offers first, then decide what to order. Most people do it the other way round — build what they want from the menu, then look for a discount that fits — and end up with a basket that qualifies for nothing.

Starting from the deals page means you are choosing between structures rather than trying to retrofit a discount onto a basket.

Step 6: Build from inside the deal tile

If you are using an offer, click into the deal and build the pizza there rather than adding items from the main menu and hoping the discount catches.

Building from the menu can leave you paying menu price for something the deal would have covered. Check that the cart shows the deal price before you pay.

Step 7: Put the most expensive qualifying item into the deal slot

A flat price buys any qualifying item for the same money, so the saving depends on which one you choose. On Mix & Match at the store we checked, a sandwich ($8.99 on the menu) saved $2.00 and 16 Bread Bites ($5.99) cost a dollar more than buying them outright.

Inside the pizza slot, use every topping the deal includes — one on the $7.99 carryout deal, two on Mix & Match — because extra ones are charged.

Step 8: Apply the free modifications

Light or extra sauce, light cheese, well-done bake, square cut. These are usually free in the online pizza builder, which shows a price if one applies. Extra cheese and extra toppings are paid.

Well done can help with a soft center on a vegetable-heavy pizza. It may not suit a barbecue-sauce base, where the sugar can catch at the edges.

Step 9: Price the basket a second way

Before checking out, rebuild the same food under a different offer structure and compare totals.

For example, two medium 1-topping pizzas plus sides might come out cheaper on the $19.99 Perfect Combo or on Mix & Match, depending on which sides you actually want. Ninety seconds of comparing is often worth a few dollars.

Step 10: Write proper delivery instructions

Gate code, buzzer number, apartment number, which entrance, anything unusual about the building.

The last fifty feet is where a delivery is most likely to go wrong: the right building, the right entrance, the right door. A driver with your gate code in the notes field does not need to call you from a spot where they have no signal.

Step 11: Check the total, not the tile price

The advertised price on a deal tile is the food. The total includes tax, delivery fee, any small-order surcharge and the tip. Look at the final number before confirming — that is the one you are actually paying.

The compressed version

  1. Domino’s own app or site.
  2. Order type first.
  3. Confirm the store.
  4. Sign in.
  5. Deals page before the menu.
  6. Build inside the deal.
  7. Most expensive qualifying item in the slot.
  8. Free modifications.
  9. Price it a second way.
  10. Real delivery instructions.
  11. Check the total.

It sounds like a lot written out. In practice it is about two minutes, and on a single large pizza it is the difference between $7.99 and more than $20.

title: The Delivery Fee Is Not a Tip: Where It Goes
excerpt: What the delivery fee covers, how drivers are generally paid, and why the two get confused at checkout.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A delivery driver handing a pizza box to a customer at her front door
keywords: does delivery fee go to driver

faqs.question: Does the pizza delivery fee go to the driver?
faqs.answer: At most chains, no. It is a store charge covering insurance, vehicle costs and operational overhead. Drivers are typically paid an hourly wage plus tips, sometimes with a small per-run reimbursement that does not resemble the fee amount.

faqs.question: How much should I tip a pizza delivery driver?
faqs.answer: A common benchmark is fifteen to twenty percent of the food total, with a floor of three to five dollars on small orders, and more in bad weather or for a difficult delivery. Percentage alone breaks down on very small orders because the driving effort is the same regardless of order size.

faqs.question: Is it better to tip in cash or on the card?
faqs.answer: Either reaches the driver at most chains, but cash reaches them the same night rather than in a future paycheck. Card tips are reliable at chain stores; cash is simply faster.

content:
At Domino’s

Each Domino’s location sets its own delivery charge, and Domino’s says that charge is not a tip for the driver. To tip, add it at online checkout or give cash at the door.

Sources: Domino’s customer FAQ; the delivery-charge disclosure was also at issue in Carpaneda v. Domino’s Pizza (D. Mass., 2014).

A common misunderstanding among people ordering delivery is that the delivery fee is the driver's payment.

It is not. Here is what is actually going on, and why the checkout screen makes it so easy to get wrong.

What the delivery fee covers

The delivery fee is a store charge. At most chains it goes to the store's operating account and covers the costs of running a delivery operation: commercial insurance, wear on company vehicles where those are used, the additional staffing that dispatch requires, and general overhead.

It is not a driver payment, it is not distributed as one, and it is not calculated as one. Its size relates to what delivery costs the store, not to what any individual driver did.

What drivers are actually paid

Typical structure at a chain store:

  • An hourly wage, which in many jurisdictions is a tipped wage below the standard minimum, topped up to the minimum if tips fall short.
  • Tips, which make up the majority of take-home pay on a good shift.
  • Sometimes a small per-delivery reimbursement toward fuel and vehicle costs when the driver uses their own car. This is usually a fraction of the delivery fee.

The practical consequence: on a slow night, a driver's income is close to the wage floor. On a busy night it is mostly tips. The delivery fee does not move with either.

Why the confusion is so persistent

Because the checkout screen puts them next to each other.

You see a line for a delivery fee and a line for a tip, adjacent, both framed as the cost of having food brought to you. It is entirely reasonable to read that as being asked to pay twice for the same service. Domino’s does say the delivery charge is not a tip, but a note like that is easy to scroll past when you are checking out in a hurry.

What this means for what you should pay

The uncomfortable version: if you reduce the tip because a delivery fee was already charged, the person absorbing that reduction is the driver. The chain's revenue is unaffected.

Rough benchmarks I would stand behind:

  • Fifteen to twenty percent of the food total as a baseline, as you would in a restaurant.
  • A floor of three to five dollars regardless of order size. A ten-dollar order takes the same drive as a forty-dollar one; percentage alone under-pays on small orders.
  • More in bad weather. Snow, ice and heavy rain make the job harder and slower, and slower means fewer runs per shift, which means less income across the whole night.
  • More for difficulty. Fourth-floor walk-up, gated complex, long driveway, unclear address — all of it costs the driver time that they are not otherwise compensated for.

Cash or card?

At a chain store, card tips reach the driver. This is worth saying clearly because a persistent rumour claims otherwise, and it costs drivers money.

The genuine difference is timing. Cash is in the driver's pocket that night. A card tip usually arrives in a future paycheck. Both reach them; one reaches them faster.

If your budget is tight

There are better places to cut than the tip, and I would rank them roughly like this:

  1. Drop the drinks. Roughly double supermarket price, and no food is lost.
  2. Switch to carryout if the store is close. No delivery, no fee, no tip owed, and usually a cheaper pizza price.
  3. Order from a bundle rather than the menu.
  4. Skip the paid extras — extra cheese, extra meat.

All four save more than trimming a tip does, and none of them come out of anyone's wages.

The one-line summary

The fee is the store's. The tip is the driver's. They are next to each other on the screen because of how checkout pages are laid out, not because they are two halves of the same payment.

What a shift actually looks like

Some context for why the tip matters as much as it does.

A driver's income is essentially tips per hour. Everything that reduces how many deliveries fit into an hour reduces income for the whole shift, not just for the delivery that was slow. A single long run to the edge of the zone can cost two shorter runs. A gated complex where nobody answers the callbox can cost ten minutes and the run behind it.

That is why weather tipping is not sentimentality. In snow, a driver might complete two-thirds of their normal runs while taking on considerably more risk. The hourly income falls at exactly the moment the job gets harder, and the only thing that offsets it is what people at the door decide to do.

Where the fee actually goes, in slightly more detail

Commercial insurance is one of the costs it is meant to cover — insuring drivers making frequent short trips in all weather is not cheap. Beyond that the fee helps pay for vehicle maintenance where the store owns cars, the additional staffing that dispatch requires, and general operating overhead.

Some stores do pay drivers a small per-delivery reimbursement toward fuel and wear when the driver uses their own car. It is usually a fraction of the fee, it is intended to cover costs rather than to compensate labor, and it is not a tip by any reasonable definition.

None of this makes the fee unreasonable. Delivery does cost the store money. It just is not the driver's money, and that is easy to miss at checkout.

title: The Mix and Match Deal, Explained Properly
excerpt: The two-items-for-a-flat-price offer is the most flexible Domino’s deal and the easiest to use badly. Here is how to extract the most from it.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Several pizzas, breadsticks, wings and salads spread across a table

faqs.question: What counts as a qualifying item in a mix and match deal?
faqs.answer: At Domino’s the reported list includes a medium 2-topping pizza, pasta, oven-baked sandwiches and Stuffed Cheesy Bread, among others. Drinks are not on it, and the full list is on the deal tile at your store.

faqs.question: Which items give the best value in a mix and match?
faqs.answer: The items with the highest standalone menu price relative to what the store spends producing them — cheesy bread over plain breadsticks, a fully topped pizza over a plain one, baked pasta over a dessert.

faqs.question: Can I order more than two items on a mix and match deal?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and the flat rate applies to each additional qualifying item. For groups it competes with the $19.99 Perfect Combo, and you control exactly what goes in.

content:
The mix and match — pick any two or more qualifying items, each at one flat price — is one of the most common deal structures in chain pizza, and the one where the gap between using it well and using it badly is widest.

Two people can order the same number of items under the same offer and one of them can walk away with substantially more food. Here is how that happens.

How the offer is constructed

The chain defines a list of qualifying items and a single price that applies to any of them. From your side that looks like a discount. From the store's side it is a weighted average: some items on that list cost far less to produce than others, and the flat price is set knowing roughly how often each gets chosen.

Which means the offer is priced around the typical selection. Choose atypically and you come out ahead.

Rule one: pick the items with the highest standalone price

Mix & Match prices every qualifying item at $6.99. At the store we checked, 16 Bread Bites cost $5.99 on the menu and Stuffed Cheesy Bread $8.49 — so the cheesy bread extracts $2.50 more from the same slot, and the Bread Bites are actually cheaper bought outside the deal.

Applied across a whole basket:

  • Cheesy bread over plain breadsticks.
  • A two-topping pizza over a plain cheese one, where the deal allows two toppings.
  • Baked pasta or a sandwich over a dessert, since desserts usually carry the lowest standalone price on the list.
  • Boneless chicken over wings, if your store’s list includes both — more meat per dollar, since there is no bone weight.

Rule two: check what is excluded before you plan the order

The exclusions are where these offers quietly get worse:

The qualifying list is set by each store, and it is shown inside the deal tile once you have entered your address. Before you plan the order, check three things there:

Pizza: the slot is a medium with up to two toppings. A third topping, a specialty pizza or a crust change can add a charge on top of $6.99; the cart shows it before you pay.

Chicken: whether wings or boneless chicken are on your store’s list. If they are not, the $7.99 carryout deal is the other way to get wings for less than the $10.99 menu price.

Drinks: we did not see drinks listed as Mix & Match items in the reports we used.

Rule three: use more than two slots when it suits you

Mix & Match does not stop at two. The $6.99 price applies to each additional qualifying item, which makes it competitive with the $19.99 Perfect Combo for a group.

The advantage over the Perfect Combo is control. The combo fixes the order — two medium 1-topping pizzas and two sides — whereas four Mix & Match slots can be four pizzas, or two pizzas and two pastas, or whatever the table actually wants.

Price both. For four or more items they land close together often enough that it is worth thirty seconds.

Rule four: this is where a two-medium order makes sense

At standard menu prices, one large pizza is better value per square inch than two mediums. Under a flat-rate mix and match, that reverses: two mediums at a flat rate each give roughly forty-five percent more total pizza than a single large, for a predictable price.

This is the specific situation where the usual size-up advice does not apply, and it is worth knowing which situation you are in.

Rule five: watch what happens to the total

Two items at $6.99 is $13.98 of food, before tax, delivery fee and tip. On a delivery order that can become twenty dollars or more by the time you confirm.

The deal is real; the tile price is not the total. This is not specific to mix and match, but the flat per-item framing makes it especially easy to under-estimate where you will land.

A worked example

Same offer, two ways of using it. Three items at $6.99 each, $20.97 either way, using menu prices from the store we checked:

Used carelessly: a medium cheese pizza (about $11.99, our estimate), 16 Bread Bites ($5.99) and a Chicken Alfredo Pasta ($8.49). Menu value $26.47.

Used deliberately: a medium 2-topping pizza (about $14.99, our estimate), Stuffed Cheesy Bread ($8.49) and an Italian sandwich ($8.99). Menu value $32.47.

Same price, same number of items, six dollars of difference. That is the entire skill involved.

The summary

  • Fill each slot with the highest standalone-price qualifying item you will actually eat.
  • Check the exclusion and surcharge list before planning.
  • Use extra slots for a group rather than defaulting to a fixed combo.
  • Two mediums beat one large under a flat rate, unlike at menu prices.
  • Judge the deal on the checkout total, not the tile.

Why chains keep this offer running

The mix and match survives every promotional refresh because it solves a problem specific to pizza economics: the store wants your basket to contain more than one item.

A single-pizza order and a three-item order consume almost the same fixed costs — the same order handling, the same oven cycle window, the same delivery run. The marginal cost of adding breadsticks to a bag that is already going out is very small. So an offer that pushes a one-item basket to a three-item basket improves the store's return on that delivery substantially, even at a discounted price per item.

Which is why the flat rate is often surprisingly good. The chain is not being generous; it is buying basket size, and basket size is worth more to it than the margin it gave up.

Ordering for one person

The obvious objection to a multi-item deal is that you are one person and do not want three items.

Two things worth knowing. First, the qualifying list includes items that can be refrigerated and reheated, such as boneless chicken and pan pizza. A two-item deal for one person is frequently two meals rather than one oversized one.

Second, if it is not worth it, the flat carryout offer on a single pizza exists precisely for this case and beats the bundle comfortably at one item. The mistake is assuming the promoted deal is the right deal for your order — it is the right deal for the average order, which is not the same thing.

Wondering whether there is a cheaper time of day to use it? See our guide to Domino’s happy hour.

title: Which Pizza Toppings Are Worth Paying For?
excerpt: Most toppings cost the same at checkout, and they are emphatically not worth the same. A ranking based on what you actually get.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A pizza with peppers, mushrooms and olives on a board, with bowls of toppings behind it

faqs.question: Do all pizza toppings cost the same?
faqs.answer: At most chains, yes — a flat per-topping charge that scales with pizza size, regardless of whether you choose mushrooms or bacon. Since the charge is uniform but the value clearly is not, meat toppings extract more from each charge than vegetables do.

faqs.question: Is extra cheese worth the money?
faqs.answer: Rarely, as a paid modification. It is one of the more expensive add-ons and the difference is often barely visible on a well-made pizza. A specialty pizza inside a deal usually delivers more for the same money.

faqs.question: How many toppings before a specialty pizza is cheaper?
faqs.answer: Usually three or four on a large, depending on your store's per-topping rate. Past that point a specialty pizza carrying five or six toppings is frequently cheaper than a custom one carrying four.

content:
At Domino’s

By our estimate one topping adds about $1.50 to a large (pepperoni $15.49 est. against $13.99 checked for cheese). Every large specialty pizza was $19.99 in our check, so a fourth topping brings a build-your-own large level with a specialty — and the ExtravaganZZa carries nine.

Checked prices: Domino’s, 628 N High St, Columbus, OH, 25 October 2026. Your store may differ.

Most chain pizza toppings are priced as a single flat charge per topping, scaled by pizza size. Mushrooms cost what bacon costs. Onions cost what sausage costs.

That uniform pricing is convenient for the store and slightly absurd for you, because the ingredients differ enormously in what they cost to buy, how much of them arrives on the pizza, and how much they change the eating experience.

Here is a ranking, and the reasoning behind it.

The best value toppings

1. Pepperoni

The most popular topping in the country, for a reason. It arrives in genuine quantity, it changes the flavor of the whole pizza, and it is the topping most likely to be included free inside a deal because offers are modeled around it.

2. Italian sausage

Applied in substantial pieces, high in flavor, and it renders fat into the cheese during the bake, which spreads the effect across the whole slice rather than concentrating it where the pieces sit.

3. Bacon

Strong flavor per gram, so even a modest quantity registers. It also crisps in the oven, adding texture that most toppings do not.

4. Extra pepperoni on an existing pepperoni pizza

Unusual entry, but sound: it is a paid change where you know exactly what the extra money buys.

Middling value

5. Grilled chicken

Decent quantity and genuine protein, but mild — it needs a sauce that carries it, which is why chicken appears on barbecue and buffalo bases rather than plain tomato.

6. Mushrooms

Applied generously and they do change the character of a pizza. But they release water during the bake and can soften the base, particularly on thin crust. Order well done if you use them.

7. Black olives

Assertive flavor, so a small quantity does work. Divisive, though, which limits their usefulness on a shared pizza.

Poor value

8. Onions

Cheap to buy, applied in moderate quantity, and they largely melt into the background during the bake. Perfectly nice; barely detectable as a paid addition.

9. Green peppers

Similar problem, plus a high water content that works against the base. On a heavily topped pizza you will struggle to identify them at all.

10. Diced tomato

Adding tomato to a tomato-sauce base. The pizza is already tomato-flavored, and fresh tomato mostly adds moisture.

11. Extra cheese

Consistently the weakest paid modification. It is one of the more expensive add-ons and, on a pizza that already carries a full cheese covering, the difference is frequently invisible. If you want a richer pizza, a meat topping does more for the same money.

The rule that matters more than the ranking

Count your toppings before you check out.

Because each topping carries a flat charge that scales with size, a build-your-own with four toppings on a large comes to about the same as a specialty pizza carrying more — roughly $19.99 by our estimate of $1.50 a topping, against $19.99 checked for a specialty. The specialty section is a pre-bundled topping discount, and past three toppings it usually wins.

It is an easy way to overspend, and it takes thirty seconds to check.

The free modifications, which are underused

These are usually free in the online pizza builder, which shows a price if one applies:

  • Well done. Can help with a soft center on a vegetable-heavy pizza. It may not suit a barbecue base, where the sugar can catch.
  • Light sauce. Can help a thin crust stay crisper.
  • Extra sauce. Changes the balance of sauce to cheese.
  • Light cheese. A genuine calorie reduction that also lets the toppings come through.
  • Removing a topping from a specialty pizza. Free, where adding one is not. Subtracting is the cheap way to customize.

A note on nutrition

Since I edit the nutrition side of this site, the honest note: vegetable toppings add very little to the calorie count and meat toppings add meaningfully — roughly twenty to forty calories per slice for a meat topping against ten or so for a vegetable.

So the value ranking and the nutrition ranking point in opposite directions, which is entirely predictable. If calories are the priority, the crust choice is a much bigger lever than the toppings: switching to thin crust saves about 80 calories a slice on a large, roughly what dropping two or three meat toppings would.

The short version

Meats extract the most from a flat per-topping charge. Vegetables mostly do not. Extra cheese is the weakest paid add-on on the board. And past three toppings, check the specialty menu before you pay for a fourth.

Why the flat per-topping charge exists

Charging the same for mushrooms and bacon is obviously not cost-based. It is interface-based.

A build-your-own ordering flow with per-ingredient pricing would require the customer to evaluate thirty prices while assembling a pizza, and every additional decision at that point in the flow loses orders. One number that applies to everything is faster to understand, faster to click through and much easier to describe in a deal.

So the store prices toppings as an average and accepts that some customers extract more from the charge than others. Being one of the customers who extracts more costs nothing except knowing which is which.

Half-and-half, the underused option

One structural point that beats any individual topping choice: you can split one pizza into two halves with different toppings, instead of buying two pizzas.

That has a useful consequence. Two half-and-half larges cover four different topping combinations for the price of two pizzas plus whatever the toppings add, which is almost always better for a mixed table than buying four smalls or ordering one supreme that half the table tolerates rather than enjoys.

It also lets you put an expensive specialty on one half and something plain on the other without paying the full specialty price twice. For a household where one person wants a loaded meat pizza and another wants cheese, this is the single most useful thing on this page.

title: Domino’s Gluten-Free Crust: What to Know Before You Order
excerpt: A gluten-free crust is not the same as a gluten-free kitchen. What that distinction means depends entirely on why you are avoiding gluten.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A vegetable pizza on a plate, with a plain round of dough on a board behind it

faqs.question: Is chain gluten-free pizza safe for celiac disease?
faqs.answer: Most chains explicitly state it is not, because the crust is prepared in a kitchen where wheat flour is airborne and shared surfaces and utensils are used. The crust itself is made without gluten ingredients; the environment is not gluten-free, and chains are generally clear about this distinction.

faqs.question: Does gluten-free crust cost more?
faqs.answer: Usually a few dollars more than a standard base, and it is commonly excluded from deal pricing or carries an upcharge inside it. It is also typically only available in one size, most often a small or medium.

faqs.question: Which pizza toppings contain gluten?
faqs.answer: Most standard toppings do not, but seasoned meats and sauces are the ones to check — some contain wheat-based binders or thickeners. Request current allergen information from the chain rather than assuming, since suppliers and recipes change.

content:
At Domino’s

Domino’s has sold a Gluten Free Crust in the US since 2012, launched in a small 10-inch size only. Domino’s own statement says the pizza is “prepared in a common kitchen with the risk of gluten exposure” and that it does not recommend it for customers with celiac disease.

We have not confirmed whether the size or price has changed since launch — check the crust options in your store’s app. Sources: Domino’s 2012 announcement (PR Newswire); Beyond Celiac.

I want to start with the distinction that matters most, because everything else on this page depends on it.

A gluten-free crust means the crust was made without gluten-containing ingredients. It does not mean the pizza was made in a gluten-free environment. At a pizza chain, those two things are very far apart, and the chains themselves are generally clear about it in their own allergen documentation — the clarity just tends to be in a footnote rather than on the menu.

Why a pizza kitchen is a difficult environment

Consider what happens in the twenty feet behind the counter. Wheat flour is used to stop dough sticking, which means it is airborne. Dough is stretched on shared surfaces. The same cutting wheel goes through every pizza. Pizzas travel through the same conveyor oven, where crumbs from earlier bakes remain. Staff handle wheat dough and then handle your toppings.

A store can put a certified gluten-free base into that environment and it will pick up trace gluten. That is not negligence; it is a physical property of the room. Eliminating it would require a separate prep area, separate utensils, separate oven and separate staff — which is why the restaurants that can serve celiac customers are dedicated gluten-free kitchens, and a pizza chain is not one.

What that means for you, specifically

The right answer depends on why you avoid gluten.

If you have celiac disease

Most chains state directly that they do not recommend their gluten-free crust for people with celiac disease. Take that at face value. It is not a legal hedge on a product that would actually be fine; it is an accurate description of the kitchen.

The amount of gluten that triggers an immune response in celiac disease is very small, and trace cross-contact in a flour-heavy kitchen is realistically unavoidable. A dedicated gluten-free kitchen, or cooking at home, is the safer route.

If you have non-celiac gluten sensitivity

This is where individual tolerance varies. Some people find a chain gluten-free crust perfectly manageable; others react to the trace exposure. Only you can calibrate that, and the honest advice is to try it once when the consequences of being wrong are low rather than before an important day.

If you are avoiding gluten by preference

Then trace cross-contact is not a health concern and the crust is simply a menu choice. Order it if you prefer it.

If you have a wheat allergy

Treat this with the same caution as celiac disease, or more. An allergic reaction can be triggered by trace exposure and the consequences are acute rather than cumulative.

The practical details

Size. Gluten-free bases are usually available in one size only, most often a small or medium. Planning to feed a group from one is not realistic.

Price. A few dollars above a standard base, and frequently excluded from deal pricing or surcharged inside it. Assume it will not be covered by whatever offer you were planning to use.

Texture. Gluten-free crusts are generally denser than wheat dough, so do not expect it to match a hand-tossed base.

Toppings. Most are gluten-free, but seasoned meats and some sauces can contain wheat-based binders or thickeners. This varies by chain and by supplier, and suppliers change. Request current allergen information rather than relying on a list you read a year ago.

Reducing risk if you order anyway

If you have decided the risk level suits you, these help at the margins:

  • Order at a quiet time. A kitchen at a Friday dinner peak is under more time pressure than the same kitchen on a quiet weekday afternoon.
  • State the reason. Saying it is for a medical requirement rather than a preference lets the store tell you plainly what it can and cannot do — and some stores may take extra care, though you should not assume it.
  • Ask for it uncut. The shared cutting wheel is a documented cross-contact point, and cutting it yourself at home removes it entirely.
  • Keep the toppings simple. Fewer ingredients means fewer opportunities for a wheat-containing component to be present.

The bottom line

Chain gluten-free crusts are a real product that fills a real need for people avoiding gluten by preference or with mild sensitivity. For celiac disease and wheat allergy, the chains' own guidance says not to rely on them, and that guidance is correct.

The crust is gluten-free. The kitchen is not. Which one matters more depends entirely on you.

Reading a chain's own allergen documentation

If you are going to rely on anything, rely on the chain's own allergen statement rather than on a menu description or a summary like this one. A few things to look for when you do.

Check the date on the document. Supplier changes happen, formulations get revised, and an allergen sheet that has not been updated in two years is describing a kitchen that may no longer exist.

Look for the language about preparation environment specifically, not just about ingredients. A statement that a crust contains no gluten ingredients and a statement that a crust is safe for celiac disease are very different claims, and most chains are careful to make only the first one. That carefulness is informative.

Check whether the statement covers the whole order or only the crust. Toppings, sauces and dips are frequently documented separately.

What has actually improved

It is worth acknowledging that gluten-free options at chains are better than they were. A decade ago the choice was frequently nothing at all; now most major chains carry a base that is a reasonable product rather than an apology.

What has not changed, and structurally cannot without a separate kitchen, is the cross-contact question. That is a building problem rather than a recipe problem, and no amount of supplier improvement addresses it.

So the honest summary is that the ingredient side of this has largely been solved and the environment side has not. Which of those matters to you determines whether the option is useful or irrelevant, and that is a decision only you can make.

title: Vegetarian and Vegan Options at Domino’s, and What to Check
excerpt: Vegetarian is straightforward at most pizza chains. Vegan is not, and the reason is the cheese — plus a couple of ingredients people rarely think to check.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A vegetable pizza with peppers and tomatoes on a plate

faqs.question: Is chain pizza dough vegan?
faqs.answer: The standard dough at most chains is made without animal ingredients, but stuffed, buttered and some flavored crusts frequently contain dairy. Verify the specific crust rather than assuming that dough in general is safe.

faqs.question: Does Domino’s have vegan cheese in the US?
faqs.answer: Not as of November 2026. Domino’s offers vegan cheese in the UK, Spain, Germany, Switzerland and Australia, but not in the US; PETA paused its campaign for a US version in January 2026 and no launch has been reported.

faqs.question: Is the tomato pizza sauce vegetarian?
faqs.answer: Standard tomato pizza sauce usually is, but creamy and alfredo-style sauces contain dairy, and some barbecue and specialty sauces contain animal-derived ingredients. The base sauce is the item most worth checking after the cheese.

content:
At Domino’s in the US

There is no vegan cheese on the US menu as of November 2026.
