Domino’s offers one in the UK, Spain, Germany, Switzerland and Australia, and PETA paused its campaign for a US version in January 2026 after Domino’s rebrand, with no US launch reported. Vegetarian ordering is straightforward; vegan means a no-cheese pizza and checking each item.

Sources: PETA (January 2026); vegconomist. Ingredients change — check the allergen and ingredient information in your store’s app before ordering.

Ordering vegetarian at a pizza chain is easy. Ordering vegan is a research project. The gap between those two experiences is almost entirely about cheese, with a few smaller traps around the edges.

Vegetarian: mostly straightforward

Every chain menu has at least one vegetable pizza, and any pizza can have its meat removed at no charge — removal is free where addition is not, which is worth remembering generally.

Two things are still worth checking.

The cheese. Some cheeses are made with animal rennet and some with microbial rennet. Which one a chain uses varies by supplier and can vary by region within the same chain. If you avoid animal rennet, this needs confirming rather than assuming.

The dough conditioner. Some commercial dough formulations include ingredients that are not vegetarian. This is uncommon but not unheard of, and it is not something you can determine by looking at the pizza.

For most people ordering vegetarian by preference rather than by strict rule, the vegetable pizzas on any chain menu are fine and this level of checking is unnecessary. For anyone who does need certainty, ask the chain for their current ingredient information — the answer changes when suppliers change.

Vegan: considerably harder

The core problem is that pizza is a cheese delivery system, and removing the cheese leaves you with sauce on bread.

Cheese alternatives

At Domino’s in the US there is none, so a vegan Domino’s pizza is a no-cheese pizza. At other chains availability is inconsistent and can vary store to store, so confirm before building an order.

Where it is unavailable, a no-cheese pizza with a generous topping load and extra sauce is a legitimate order. Some people add a well-done bake, since without cheese there is nothing between the sauce and the toppings.

The dough

Standard pizza dough at most chains is made without animal ingredients. The exceptions cluster in the specialty crusts — stuffed crusts, buttered rims and some flavored bases frequently contain dairy.

The garlic butter brushed onto breadsticks and pizza rims after baking is a specific and easily-missed one. It is often genuine dairy butter.

The sauces

Standard tomato sauce is usually fine. Creamy and alfredo-style sauces are not. Some barbecue and specialty sauces contain animal-derived ingredients, most often honey or dairy solids.

The sides

Most bread sides carry cheese, butter or both. Plain breadsticks may be brushed with dairy butter even without a cheese topping. Check desserts too, because dairy and egg are common in them.

A realistic vegan order

A starting point to confirm with your store:

  • Standard hand-tossed or thin crust base, confirmed dairy-free.
  • Standard tomato sauce, ordered extra.
  • Plant-based cheese if stocked; no cheese if not.
  • A heavy vegetable load — mushrooms, peppers, onions, olives, tomato — since without cheese the toppings carry the whole pizza.
  • Well done.
  • Skip the sides, or check each one individually rather than assuming.

On cross-contact

The same principle applies here as with gluten: a pizza kitchen is a shared environment. The same surfaces, cutters and oven handle meat and dairy all day.

For most people avoiding animal products by ethical or dietary preference, this is not a health issue and is generally accepted as unavoidable in a non-vegan kitchen. For anyone with a dairy allergy, it is a genuine safety consideration and should be treated the way any allergy is — trace exposure is possible and a chain pizza kitchen cannot rule it out.

Where the industry is going

Plant-based cheese availability at chains has broadened over recent years but remains patchy, and it is the constraint on everything else. The vegetable toppings have always been there; the dough is usually fine; the missing piece has consistently been a cheese that melts acceptably and that stores are willing to stock.

Until availability becomes consistent, the practical advice is unchanged: check your specific store first, and build the order around what it actually carries rather than what the national menu suggests.

Ordering a good no-cheese pizza

If your store does not stock a plant-based cheese, a no-cheese pizza is the fallback, and it can be good rather than merely acceptable — but only if you order it deliberately.

Cheese does two jobs on a pizza beyond taste: it binds the toppings to the base and it acts as a moisture barrier. Remove it and both jobs go unfilled, which is why a plain no-cheese pizza often arrives as a dry base with toppings sliding off it.

Three adjustments fix most of that. Ask for extra sauce, which restores moisture and gives the toppings something to sit in. A well-done bake is an option if you want a firmer base. And load the toppings heavily — with no cheese to carry the pizza, the vegetables have to do all the work.

A drizzle of oil after it arrives, and something acidic on the table, closes most of the remaining gap.

What to ask when you call

If you need to check ingredients with a store rather than relying on published information, asking about specific items gets a far better answer than asking whether something is vegan. “Is it vegan?” depends on definitions, so a question about a specific ingredient is easier to answer accurately.

Useful questions: does the dough contain any dairy or animal-derived ingredient; is the garlic butter on the breadsticks real butter; is the standard tomato sauce dairy-free; do you stock a plant-based cheese today. Four concrete answers beat one vague reassurance.

title: Pizza Calories: Which Choices Actually Change the Number
excerpt: Some pizza decisions move the calorie count substantially and some barely register. Here is which is which, ranked by impact.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A cut vegetable pizza on a board with a glass of water and a bowl of basil
keywords: how many calories in a slice of pizza

pricing.label: Calories per slice, large pizza
pricing.note: Thin-crust cheese (about 210, our estimate) at the low end; Spicy Chicken Bacon Ranch (410, as listed in the official cart) at the high end.

faqs.question: How many calories are in a slice of pizza?
faqs.answer: At Domino’s, roughly 210 to 410 for a slice of a large pizza cut into eight. Thin-crust cheese (about 210, our estimate) sits at the bottom; the hand-tossed cheese slice is 290 and the specialty pizzas run from 310 to 410 in the official cart.

faqs.question: What is the biggest calorie saving on a chain pizza?
faqs.answer: Switching a large from hand tossed to thin crust, which removes roughly 80 calories a slice (290 to about 210) while leaving the toppings untouched. Thin crust is usually priced the same as hand tossed (our thin-crust prices are estimates), which makes it the largest low-cost reduction available.

faqs.question: Does light cheese make a meaningful difference?
faqs.answer: Yes — cheese is one of the largest single contributors on a pizza, and requesting light cheese is usually a free option in the online pizza builder. Combined with thin crust it can take a slice down substantially without removing a topping.

content:
At Domino’s

Per slice of a large hand-tossed pizza, as listed in the Domino’s cart we checked: cheese 290, Pacific Veggie and Philly Cheese Steak 310, Memphis BBQ Chicken 350, MeatZZa 360, ExtravaganZZa 370. Crunchy thin is about 210 by our estimate.

Use Domino’s own nutrition calculator for your exact order; toppings, crust and size all change the number.

Pizza has a reputation as a single monolithic unhealthy food, which is not a useful way to think about it. A slice of thin-crust vegetable pizza and a slice of pan-crust meat pizza can differ by well over 100 calories, and they came from the same menu.

Here is what actually moves the number, in order of how much it moves it.

1. The crust — the largest single lever

Per slice of a plain cheese pizza cut into eight:

  • Crunchy thin, large: about 210 calories (our estimate from published nutrition data)
  • Hand tossed, large: 290 calories, as listed in the official cart
  • Handmade pan, medium: about 280 calories (estimate) — and a medium slice is smaller, so pan is the heaviest crust for its size

Switching a large from hand tossed to thin removes roughly 80 calories per slice with the toppings unchanged. Across three slices, that is close to a whole slice of pizza.

What makes this the most useful intervention is that it is free and it removes nothing you wanted. Nobody orders a pizza for the dough.

2. Cheese

Cheese is the second-largest contributor and one of the few that is both substantial and free to reduce. Light cheese is usually a free option in the online pizza builder.

Extra cheese, correspondingly, is one of the largest paid increases available, in both price and calories.

3. Meat toppings

Roughly 20 to 40 calories per slice per meat topping on a large, by our estimate. In the cart we checked, the MeatZZa — four meats plus extra cheese — was 360 calories a slice against 290 for plain cheese: about 70 more, less than adding up the toppings one by one would suggest.

Vegetable toppings, by contrast, add around 5 to 15 calories per slice. Loading a pizza with vegetables changes the calorie count very little and improves the pizza considerably, which makes it one of the better trades on the menu.

4. How many slices you eat

Not a menu decision, but it dominates all of the above.

Three slices of a large MeatZZa is about 1,080 calories (360 each, as listed in the cart). Three slices of a thin-crust cheese pizza is about 630. But five slices of the thin crust is over a thousand again, and a lighter pizza is easier to eat more of.

We mention this because the practical failure mode of ordering the lighter option is eating more of it. If that is your pattern, ordering a smaller pizza is more effective than ordering a lighter one.

5. Sides and drinks — the invisible half

This is where people are most often surprised.

  • One piece of Stuffed Cheesy Bread is 160 calories — about half a slice of hand-tossed cheese pizza, and an order has several pieces.
  • A Chicken Alfredo Pasta is 590 calories, about two slices; the mac & cheese dishes are 830–840, nearly three.
  • A three-cake Lava Cake Flight is 1,080 calories in all — 360 per cake.
  • Regular Coke adds 140 calories per 12-ounce glass, and a two-liter bottle across an evening adds up quickly.

People carefully choose a thin crust and then order cheesy bread, pasta and dessert alongside it. The pizza may not be the largest item on that order.

What a lighter chain pizza order looks like

Not a diet plan — just the same order, built with the free levers pulled:

  • Thin crust.
  • Light cheese.
  • One meat topping rather than three, plus as many vegetables as you like.
  • Well done if you like, which does not change the calories.
  • Water or a zero-sugar drink.
  • Skip the bread side, or share one.

Against a pan-crust meat pizza with cheesy bread and soda, that is a difference of several hundred calories per person. Nothing on the list involves eating less pizza — it involves choosing differently at points where the choice was free anyway.

Some perspective

The honest take: we'd rather someone ordered pizza they enjoyed once a week than felt bad about it. The numbers on this page are for making informed choices, not for making anyone anxious about dinner.

The two useful facts are these: the crust is the biggest lever and it is free, and the sides are a bigger contributor than most people realize. Everything else is detail.

A note on the figures

All numbers here are approximate and vary by chain, region and store. Portioning at a chain store is done by hand against a target, so two pizzas built to the same specification can differ. Where a chain publishes its own nutrition information, treat that as authoritative over any general guide including this one.

Why published figures and your pizza differ

A short note on precision, because the numbers on this page look more exact than they are.

Portioning at a chain store is done by hand against a target. The amount of cheese and toppings can vary from one pizza to the next. Published nutrition figures describe the specification, not the pizza in front of you.

That variation is not a reason to ignore the numbers — the difference between a thin-crust vegetable pizza and a pan meat pizza dwarfs any portioning variance. It is a reason not to treat a fifteen-calorie difference between two options as meaningful. Use the figures for the big decisions and ignore them for the small ones.

What actually helps, if you order regularly

Three habits, in order of how much difference they make for someone eating chain pizza most weeks:

  • Decide how many slices before the box opens. This dominates every menu choice on this page. Portioning onto a plate rather than eating from the box is unglamorous and effective.
  • Default to thin crust unless you have a reason not to. It is free, it removes nothing you wanted, and over a month of regular ordering it adds up substantially.
  • Treat the sides as food, not as extras. Cheesy bread and a baked pasta alongside a pizza is two meals arriving as one, and it is where most of the surprise in a takeout calorie count lives.

None of that involves eating pizza less often, which is deliberate. Advice you will not follow is not advice.

title: How Much to Tip a Pizza Delivery Driver
excerpt: Percentage rules break down on small orders. Here is a framework that holds up across order sizes, weather and distance.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A customer at her door paying by card as a driver hands over two pizza boxes
keywords: how much to tip pizza delivery

faqs.question: What is a standard tip for pizza delivery?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to twenty percent of the food total is the common benchmark, with a floor of three to five dollars on small orders. The floor matters because the driving effort is identical whether the order is ten dollars or forty.

faqs.question: Should I tip more in bad weather?
faqs.answer: Yes. Snow, ice and heavy rain make each run slower and more dangerous, which reduces how many deliveries a driver can complete across a whole shift. A few extra dollars is a reasonable acknowledgement of that.

faqs.question: Do I still tip if there is a delivery fee?
faqs.answer: Yes. At most chains the delivery fee is a store charge covering insurance and operating costs and does not go to the driver. Reducing the tip because a fee was applied takes money from the driver, not the company.

content:
At Domino’s

Domino’s says its delivery charge is not a tip, and each store sets its own charge. You can add a tip at online checkout or give cash at the door.

Source: Domino’s customer FAQ.

Tipping advice usually arrives as a percentage and stops there. Percentages are a reasonable starting point and they break down at both ends of the range, which is where most of the real questions live.

Here is a framework that holds up across those cases.

Start with the floor, not the percentage

The work of a delivery is almost identical whether your order is ten dollars or forty. Same drive, same parking, same stairs, same conversation at the door. The only thing that scales with order size is how heavy the bag is.

So a pure percentage under-pays badly on small orders. Fifteen percent of a twelve-dollar order is a dollar eighty for a fifteen-minute round trip, which is not a serious number.

Start at three to five dollars as a minimum, then apply a percentage on top for larger orders. On anything above roughly twenty-five dollars, fifteen to twenty percent will exceed the floor naturally and the percentage takes over.

Adjust for the things that cost the driver time

Time is the driver's actual currency. Tips per hour is what determines whether a shift was worth working, so anything that slows a run down reduces income across the whole night, not just on your delivery.

Add for bad weather. Snow, ice and heavy rain slow every run and make several of them unpleasant. A few extra dollars is warranted and it is noticed.

Add for distance. If you are at the edge of a delivery zone, your order is a twenty-five minute round trip rather than an eight minute one. That is two runs the driver did not do.

Add for difficulty. Fourth-floor walk-up, gated complex with a code that does not work, long unlit driveway, an apartment block where the numbering makes no sense. All of it is unpaid time.

Add for a large or awkward order. Six pizzas and four two-liter bottles is two trips from the car.

The fee is not the tip

I have written about this at length elsewhere, so briefly: at most chains the delivery fee goes to the store, not the driver. It covers insurance, vehicle costs and operational overhead.

When someone reduces a tip because they have already paid a delivery fee, the reduction comes out of the driver's income and the chain's revenue is unchanged. It is one of the most common tipping mistakes, and it is rarely made on purpose — the checkout screen simply does not explain it.

Cash or card

Both reach the driver at a chain store. There is a stubborn rumour that card tips get skimmed, and at chain stores it is not true.

The real difference is timing: cash is in their pocket that night, a card tip arrives in a future paycheck. If you have cash, it is slightly better. If you do not, tip on the card without worrying about it.

When a lower tip is reasonable

Tipping is not unconditional and I would not argue that it is. A poor delivery — wrong order, obvious rudeness, food clearly mishandled — is a fair reason to tip less.

But be sure the fault is the driver's. Things that are not:

  • The food was cold after a long journey. That is distance and queue depth.
  • The order was wrong. Assembled in the kitchen, not by the driver, who does not open the box.
  • It took an hour on a Friday night. That is the store's queue. The driver delivered it as soon as it existed.
  • The tracker said twenty minutes and it took forty. The tracker is an estimate produced by a system, not a promise made by a person.

Almost everything that goes wrong with a delivery order happens before the driver picks up the bag.

If money is tight

Fair enough, and there are better places to cut. Switch to carryout if the store is close — no delivery, no fee, no tip owed, and usually a cheaper pizza. Drop the drinks. Order from a bundle. Skip the paid extras.

All of those save more than trimming a tip does, and none of them come out of someone's wages.

The rule I would give a friend

Five dollars minimum. Twenty percent on anything substantial. More in the snow, more up stairs, more at the edge of the zone. And do not subtract for the delivery fee, because that money never reached the person standing at your door.

Tipping in advance versus at the door

A question worth addressing: does tipping when you place the order change the service you get?

Not at a chain store, and this is one of the clearer differences between chain delivery and gig-economy platforms. On an app where drivers see the payout before accepting a job, a low tip can mean your order sits unclaimed. At a chain, a salaried or hourly driver is handed a run by dispatch and delivers what they are given, in the order they are given it. A low tip does not leave your order waiting for someone to accept it.

What that means practically is that tipping at checkout and tipping at the door are equivalent in outcome. Choose whichever you find easier — though a card tip entered at checkout is one fewer thing to think about when the doorbell goes.

Group orders and large deliveries

Large orders deserve a specific mention because percentage-based tipping starts to look uncomfortable at the top end.

Twenty percent on a hundred-dollar party order is twenty dollars for one delivery, which is high by any measure. But that order is also two trips from the car, likely a scheduled slot the store worked around, and often a walk into a building rather than a doorstep handover.

Somewhere in the ten to fifteen percent range on very large orders, with a floor well above what a small order would earn, is where I would land. The principle is the same as everywhere else on this page: pay for the work, not for the food.

title: Ordering Pizza for a Group: How Much to Get
excerpt: The two mistakes are ordering too little and ordering the wrong shape of deal. Both are avoidable with about five minutes of planning.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: A group of friends reaching for slices from several pizzas on a crowded table
keywords: how many pizzas for a group

faqs.question: How many pizzas do I need for 10 people?
faqs.answer: Three to four large pizzas, depending on whether there are sides. The working rule is three slices per adult when pizza is the whole meal and two when there are sides, against eight slices per large pizza.

faqs.question: Is the Perfect Combo better than Mix & Match for a group?
faqs.answer: It can be cheaper, but it fixes the order: two medium 1-topping pizzas and the same two sides. Mix & Match at $6.99 an item often lands at a similar total while letting you choose exactly what goes in, so price both before committing.

faqs.question: How far ahead should I order for a large group?
faqs.answer: Ninety minutes on a weekend evening, or schedule it for a set time. A big order placed in the middle of a rush joins a long queue; ordering early keeps it out of the peak.

content:
Ordering pizza for ten people is a different problem from ordering for two, and the failure modes are specific: not enough food, the wrong deal structure, and food that arrives forty minutes after you needed it.

All three are solvable in advance.

How much food you actually need

The planning numbers we use across this site:

  • Pizza as the whole meal: three slices per adult.
  • Pizza with sides on the table: two slices per adult.
  • Children: one to two slices.
  • A large pizza: eight slices.

So for ten adults with sides, that is twenty slices, which is three large pizzas with a little spare. For ten adults with no sides, thirty slices, which is four larges.

Round up rather than down. Leftover pizza is a known and welcome quantity; running out in front of guests is not.

Which deal structure suits a group

Two candidates, and they are closer than people assume.

The $19.99 Perfect Combo

Two medium 1-topping pizzas, 16 Parmesan Bread Bites and 8 Cinnamon Twists for $19.99, as reported in November 2026. That is about $5 a head for four people; two combos cover eight to ten for about $40.

The catch is that the order is fixed: medium pizzas with one topping each, and the same two sides every time.

Multi-slot mix and match

Mix & Match keeps the $6.99 price for every extra qualifying item, so four medium 2-topping pizzas come to $27.96 and you choose every one. If someone can pick up and your store allows the carryout deal more than once on an order, four large 1-topping pizzas at $7.99 are $31.96 — more pizza than either.

Price both. They can land close together, so the five minutes is worthwhile; Mix & Match is the more flexible one if your group has specific requirements.

What to order for a mixed group

A mix that covers most tastes for ten to twelve people:

  • One plain cheese. There is always someone. Children, in particular.
  • One pepperoni. Pepperoni is widely reported as the most popular topping in the country.
  • One vegetable. Covers vegetarians and the people who wanted something lighter.
  • One loaded meat or specialty. For the people who came to eat.

Half-and-half pizzas are worth knowing about here: two half-and-half pizzas cover four preferences for the cost of two pizzas plus their toppings. The cart shows what each half adds.

Sides, honestly assessed

For a group, bread sides are the efficient choice — cheap, filling, universally acceptable, and they reduce how much pizza each person eats, which lets you order one fewer pizza.

Wings are the inefficient choice. Substantial bone weight, and at four to five wings per person for a group of ten you are ordering two large portions to serve as a side dish.

Drinks: buy them from a shop. A 2-liter was $4.49 in our check against roughly $2.50–3.00 in a supermarket, so on a party order with three or four bottles that is about $5–8 of pure convenience charge.

The timing, which matters more than the order

This is where group orders actually fail.

Order ninety minutes ahead on a weekend evening. A big order placed in the middle of a rush joins a long queue. Ordering early, or scheduling it, means it is not competing with everyone else’s dinner.

Use the scheduled ordering function. Domino’s lets you choose a future time for the order, which turns a large order from a gamble into an appointment.

Consider carryout for very large orders. You avoid the delivery fee and tip, and a scheduled carryout order should be ready when you arrive. Sending one person to collect is often the single biggest saving available on a party order.

Add fifteen minutes to whatever the tracker says if you are ordering into a Friday or Saturday peak, and plan the evening around the later number.

A worked example: twelve people

  • Four large pizzas — cheese, pepperoni, vegetable, meat — giving 32 slices: the 24 that twelve people need at two each with sides, plus spare.
  • Two orders of Bread Bites or Stuffed Cheesy Bread.
  • Drinks from the supermarket.
  • Priced on the $7.99 carryout deal if someone can pick up and your store allows four (about $32 for the pizzas), or as Mix & Match mediums if not.
  • Scheduled ninety minutes ahead, collected if someone can drive.

That feeds twelve people comfortably, arrives when you asked for it, and costs meaningfully less than the same food ordered at seven o'clock on the night with drinks added at checkout.

Handling dietary requirements without doubling the order

Almost every group has at least one person who cannot eat the default pizza, and the instinct is to order them a separate small one. That is usually the most expensive way to solve it.

Half-and-half is the cheaper structure. One pizza can be split into a vegetarian half and a meat half, which costs far less than a separate small pizza; the cart shows what each half’s toppings add. Two half-and-half larges cover four requirements for the price of two pizzas.

Gluten-free is the exception: at Domino’s it comes as a 10-inch small only and cannot sensibly be shared. If someone in the group needs one, order it as a separate item and read our guide on what a chain gluten-free crust does and does not mean before you do.

The mistake nobody expects

Ordering everything cold-tolerant and nothing hot-tolerant. If your food is arriving forty minutes before people eat — which is common at a party, where the food arrives before the guests are ready — the composition matters more than the quantity.

We have not timed how each item holds up. As a general rule, though, the items built around melted cheese or a molten center — cheesy bread and lava cakes — are the ones that depend most on being eaten hot.

For a party where the food will sit, weight the order toward pizza and chicken, and either skip the temperature-sensitive items or schedule them to arrive with a second, later delivery. Ordering four lava cakes ninety minutes before anyone eats dessert is money spent on a product you will not receive.

title: Late-Night Pizza: What's Open After 10pm
excerpt: Closing time and last-order time are different things, and the gap between them catches people out constantly.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A woman eating pizza from an open box at her kitchen table late at night

faqs.question: What time do pizza chains stop delivering?
faqs.answer: It varies by store. Some stop taking delivery orders a little before their posted closing time, and carryout can run slightly later. Check your store page, or call, if you are ordering close to closing time.

faqs.question: Are pizza stores open later at weekends?
faqs.answer: Usually by an hour or so on Friday and Saturday. Hours are set store by store rather than nationally, so the store two miles away can close an hour later than yours.

faqs.question: Is the food different late at night?
faqs.answer: The recipe is the same. The practical risk near closing time is that the store stops taking orders, or delivery stops, a little before the posted close — so ordering well before closing time is the safer bet.

content:
The most common late-night pizza mistake is assuming that a store listed as closing at midnight will take an order at 11:55pm. It will not, and the reason is simple once you count what has to happen before the doors close.

Closing time is not last-order time

The posted closing time is when the store shuts. The last order has to be taken, made, baked, boxed and — for delivery — driven to you and back, all before that.

So some stores stop taking delivery orders before the posted close. We have not surveyed stores for an exact cut-off, and it varies by store, so check your store page or call if you are ordering near closing time.

Carryout often runs slightly later, because there is no round trip to fit in. If you are close to the wire, switching to carryout can sometimes buy you a little time.

Hours are set per store, not nationally

Franchisees set their own hours based on local demand and staffing. This means the chain's general hours are guidance rather than fact, and two stores in the same city can differ by more than an hour.

Always check your specific store after entering your address. The national page will tell you what is typical; your store page tells you what is true.

Typical patterns

The general shape, from store pages and hours listings — check yours:

  • Weeknights: a close somewhere around 11pm to midnight is common, but plenty of stores differ.
  • Friday and Saturday: often later than weeknights.
  • Sunday: often the earliest close of the week.
  • Campus and city-center stores: can stay open later than suburban ones.

If late-night ordering is a regular thing for you, it is worth finding out which store near you keeps the latest hours once, rather than checking every time.

What actually changes in the last hour

The recipe does not change. The circumstances do.

Staffing is at its lowest. The closing crew is smaller than the dinner-rush crew, so a burst of late orders takes longer to clear than the same volume at 7pm.

Clean-down has started. Prep areas and equipment are being broken down and cleaned progressively through the last hour. That is a health requirement, not laziness, and it means a late order is being made around a partially disassembled line.

Some items may be unavailable. Where an item requires equipment that has already been cleaned, it can quietly drop off availability. Wings and pasta are the usual candidates.

Delivery zones sometimes shrink. With fewer drivers on, some stores restrict how far they will send a late run.

None of this makes a late-night pizza bad. It does mean that ordering at 11pm rather than 11:28pm gets you a noticeably better experience for no extra cost.

Late-night deals

We could not find a Domino’s late-night deal running in the US in November 2026. The everyday deals — the $7.99 carryout offer and Mix & Match — apply right up to the cut-off, and an individual store may add its own offer.

These are almost always store-level rather than national. If it is not showing on your store's deals page, your store is not running it, and no code will make it appear.

Practical advice

  • Check your specific store's hours, not the chain's general ones.
  • Leave a margin before the posted close rather than ordering in the last few minutes.
  • Order earlier rather than later if you have the choice, so there is no risk of missing a cut-off.
  • Try carryout if you have missed the delivery window. It sometimes runs later.
  • Tip well on a late run. A driver on the last delivery of the night is finishing their shift with your order and going back to clean down.

If you have missed it entirely

Once the store is closed, it is closed — there is no back door, and calling will not reach anyone. The realistic options are a twenty-four-hour store if your city has one, or scheduling an order for tomorrow, which most chains allow you to do at any hour.

The scheduling option is useful here: you can place tomorrow's lunch order at 1am when you discover the store is shut.

Why hours differ so much between nearby stores

Two stores three miles apart can close an hour apart, and the reason is entirely economic rather than corporate.

Staying open costs a franchisee real money: staff on the clock, ovens running, lights on, a driver available. That is only worth doing if the late hour generates enough orders to cover it. A store next to a university or in a city center with late-night trade clears that bar easily. A suburban store where the last order comes in at ten does not, and closing earlier is a rational decision rather than a service failure.

Which is why the answer to what time does pizza close is always store-specific, and why the national page can only ever tell you what is typical.

Ordering ahead

Domino’s lets you schedule an order for a later time, and that is particularly useful at the ends of the day.

You can place an order at one in the morning for delivery at midday tomorrow. If you have just discovered your store is closed, that is a better outcome than nothing — the order is locked in, and lunch is handled before you have got out of bed.

It also solves the opposite problem. If you know you will want food at eleven tonight and your store's last delivery order is at half past eleven, scheduling removes the risk of remembering at twenty-five past and finding the store has stopped taking orders early because the closing crew is already breaking down the line.

Hoping that ordering at a certain hour will be cheaper? Our guide to Domino’s happy hour explains what we found, and which deals save the most.

title: What the Pizza Tracker Is Actually Telling You
excerpt: The tracker is a real status display for part of the process and an estimate for the rest. Knowing which stage is which explains most of its inaccuracy.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A woman on her sofa checking her phone while a delivery arrives at the door behind her

faqs.question: Is the pizza tracker accurate?
faqs.answer: The in-store stages — order placed, prep, bake — reflect where your order is in the store. The delivery stage is where accuracy drops: the moment the driver leaves is real, and the arrival time after that is an estimate.

faqs.question: Why does the tracker say delivered before the food arrives?
faqs.answer: The status changes when the order is marked delivered, which may happen a minute or two before the handover. If it says delivered and nothing has arrived after a few minutes, call the store straight away.

faqs.question: Does the tracker show the driver's live location?
faqs.answer: Only where the store offers GPS driver tracking. Elsewhere you see a stage indicator and an estimated time instead.

content:
At Domino’s

The Domino’s Tracker follows an order through order placed, prep, bake, quality check and out for delivery. Some stores also show the driver’s position on a map once the order leaves.

Which version you see depends on your store. For a problem with an order, call the store that made it.

The order tracker is one of the more successful pieces of interface design in fast food, and it is widely misunderstood. It is not a lie, and it is also not a live feed. It is a mix of both, and knowing which stage is which explains almost every complaint people have about it.

What each stage actually is

Order placed

Real and instant. Your order hit the store's point-of-sale system.

Prep

Real: the order has reached the make line.

Bake

Mostly real, and this is the most reliable stage on the whole tracker. Conveyor ovens run at a fixed speed, so a pizza that goes in takes about the same time to come out every time. That makes bake the most predictable stage.

Quality check / boxing

Brief. It can pass so quickly that it seems to be skipped.

Out for delivery

The transition is real — a driver logged your order onto their run. Everything after that is an estimate.

This is where the accuracy drops, and it drops for a specific reason: the driver almost certainly has more than one order in the car.

Why your delivery takes longer than the estimate

A driver can carry more than one order per trip, which is part of what makes delivery pay for itself.

So when the tracker says out for delivery, your pizza might be first on a run of three or last. If it is last, it has been in the car for two other stops before it reaches you. The tracker generally cannot show that, because it is displaying your order's status, not the driver's route.

Where your store offers live GPS tracking of the driver, you can see where the car actually is. Where it does not, the delivery time is an estimate.

Why it sometimes says delivered before it arrives

The status changes when the order is marked delivered, and that can happen a minute or two before or after the handover.

Not an error, just an artifact of when the button gets pressed.

What the tracker will not tell you

This is the useful part.

How deep the queue is. Your order sitting at prep for twelve minutes on a Friday means a long queue in front of it. The tracker shows your stage, not your position.

How many stops are ahead of you. As above.

That something has gone wrong. If an order has to be remade, the tracker may not show it clearly.

Whether the store is short-staffed. Which is usually the biggest driver of a slow night, and not something the tracker shows.

How to read it usefully

  • Trust the bake stage. It is accurate and it means your food exists.
  • Treat the delivery estimate as optimistic at peak times. Add ten to fifteen minutes on a Friday or Saturday evening.
  • A long prep stage means a queue, not a problem. Nothing is wrong; there are simply orders ahead of yours.
  • Call the store if it has been stuck for a long time. Twenty minutes on one stage with no movement is worth a phone call, and phone staff can see the actual order record rather than the customer-facing summary.

Why it exists at all

Because waiting with information is more tolerable than waiting without it. The tracker does not make pizza arrive faster; it makes the same wait easier to plan around.

That is a real product improvement even though nothing about the pizza changed. Just do not mistake the delivery estimate for a promise — the in-store stages are a status display, and the last one is a forecast.

What to do when the tracker stalls

A practical decision tree, since this is the situation people actually find themselves in.

Stuck at prep for more than fifteen minutes. Almost certainly a queue. Frustrating, not broken. On a Friday evening this is normal and calling will not move you up the list.

Stuck at bake for more than ten minutes. Unusual, because bake is the predictable stage. Worth a call to ask what is happening.

Out for delivery for more than forty minutes. You are probably last on a multi-stop run, or your address is at the edge of the zone. If it passes an hour, call the store.

Marked delivered but nothing arrived. Call immediately rather than waiting. The most common causes are a neighboring address or a drop-off at a door you do not use, and both are much easier to resolve in the first ten minutes.

Why phoning the store beats phoning anyone else

The store is where your order actually is, so the people there are best placed to tell you what is happening with it.

A national customer service line is further from your order, so going straight to the store is usually the quicker route to an answer.

title: Domino's Christmas Availability 2026: Is It Open?
excerpt: Is Domino's open on Christmas? What the company has said, what to expect on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, and how to confirm your own store's hours.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A lit Christmas tree and wrapped presents beside the title Domino’s Christmas Availability 2026

faqs.question: Is Domino's open on Christmas Day 2026?
faqs.answer: It depends on the store. Domino's has said it does not require stores to open on Christmas Day, and franchise owners decide for themselves. Some stores may open with reduced hours, but plan on yours being closed until the store confirms otherwise.

faqs.question: Is Domino's open on Christmas Eve?
faqs.answer: Usually, though often with shorter hours. Christmas Eve 2026 is a Thursday. Stores are not required to open, so confirm your store's hours on the Domino's app or website, or by phone.

faqs.question: What time does Domino's close on Christmas Eve?
faqs.answer: There is no national closing time. Each store sets its own, and many close earlier than usual. Some stores stop delivery before the posted close, so order well before then.

faqs.question: Does Domino's deliver on Christmas Day?
faqs.answer: Only where a store is open and has drivers working. A store that is open may offer carryout only or limit its delivery area, so check your address in the app or call the store.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my Domino's is open on Christmas?
faqs.answer: Enter your address on dominos.com or in the app to find the store that serves you, check its hours for the date, then call the store to confirm. Calling on December 22 or 23 gives you time to change your plans.

faqs.question: Why is one Domino's open on Christmas when another nearby is closed?
faqs.answer: Most US Domino's stores are franchise-owned, and each owner sets holiday hours based on staff and local demand. Two nearby stores can have different owners and make different decisions.

faqs.question: Are Domino's deals available on Christmas?
faqs.answer: If your store is open, it may still run offers, but franchisees choose which promotions they join. Check your own store's deals page after entering your address rather than relying on an advertised offer.

faqs.question: Is Domino's open the day after Christmas?
faqs.answer: Most stores should be back to regular hours on December 26, which is a Saturday in 2026, though a late opening is possible. Your store page has the final answer.

content:
Quick answer

Domino’s has no single Christmas schedule. Christmas Day availability is decided store by store — plan on your store being closed until it confirms otherwise. Christmas Eve is the safer bet, but many stores close early.

Christmas 2026 falls on a Friday. As of November 4, 2026, we could not find a chain-wide Domino’s holiday schedule for this year, so anything promising exact hours for every store should be treated with suspicion.

Search “is Domino’s open on Christmas” and you will find pages saying yes, pages saying no, and pages listing exact hours for the whole country. They cannot all be right, and the reason they disagree is simple: there is no national answer. This guide sets out what Domino’s has actually said about Christmas availability, what to expect on each day, and how to get a definite answer for your own store in about two minutes.

What Domino’s says about Christmas hours

The company’s position has been consistent whenever reporters have asked. A Domino’s spokesperson told CBS News that the chain does not require stores to stay open on Christmas Day and pointed customers to the website for local hours. Another told Newsweek that stores “are not mandated to be open on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day”, noting that most US stores are franchise-owned.

Stores “decide on the holiday hours for each of their stores based on what works for their store teams and local communities.”

— Domino’s spokesperson, quoted by Good Housekeeping, 2022

That is why a store two miles from you can be open while yours is dark. The owner of each store weighs staffing against local demand and makes the call, and it can change from one year to the next — so last year’s experience is a clue, not a promise.

Domino’s Christmas availability, day by day

This is the pattern to plan around for 2026. It is a guide to what is likely, not the hours of any particular store.

Thu, Dec 24

Christmas Eve

Usually open, shorter hours

Reports generally describe stores opening but closing early. One store’s holiday notice listed an 8pm close; yours may differ. Order before dinnertime.

Fri, Dec 25

Christmas Day

Varies — assume closed

The owner’s decision. Some stores open with reduced hours and many do not. Confirm with your store before you count on it.

Sat, Dec 26

Day after Christmas

Expect a return to normal

Many stores are likely to be on regular hours, but a late opening is possible, so check.

What about closing time?

Even when a store is open, the posted closing time is not your deadline. Many stores stop taking delivery orders before they close, because the driver has to get back before the store shuts, while carryout can run later. Check the order cut-off on your store page, or call, rather than assuming you can order right up to the posted closing time. Our hours and last-order guide has a table for every closing time.

How to check your store’s Christmas hours

This takes about two minutes, and the order matters: start with the sources closest to the store.

  1. Enter your address on the official site or app. Open dominos.com or the Domino’s app and enter your delivery address. This shows the store that actually serves you, which is not always the nearest one — here is why.
  2. Look at that store’s hours for the date itself. Check again in the days before Christmas, because holiday changes may not appear weeks ahead.
  3. Check delivery and carryout separately. A store can be open for carryout after delivery has stopped. If delivery is unavailable, switch to carryout before you give up.
  4. Call the store. It is the only answer guaranteed to be current. Ask three things: are you open on the 25th, what time do you stop taking orders, and are you delivering to my address?
  5. Do not rely on a search listing alone. Map and search results are handy, but they can lag behind one-off holiday changes.

Best time to ask: call on December 22 or 23, during a quiet part of the afternoon. By then the store is more likely to know its holiday hours, and you still have time to change your plans.

What changes when a store does open

Holiday availability is not only about whether the doors are open. Four things are worth expecting on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day:

  • Fewer drivers, longer waits. A store running with a smaller team can take longer per order, and with few other restaurants open, demand can land on the stores that are. Order earlier than you normally would.
  • Smaller delivery areas. With fewer drivers on, a store may limit how far it delivers. Carryout gets around that, and it also skips the fee and tip — here is what that saves.
  • Different deals. Franchisees opt into promotions one by one, so check your own store’s deals page rather than assuming an advertised offer applies. Our coupons and deals guide explains the offer types.
  • Tipping matters more. Whoever brings your food is working Christmas. If you can, tip above your usual amount — our tipping guide gives a sensible baseline.

If your Domino’s is closed on Christmas

The most reliable plan is not to need the store on the 25th at all. Order on Christmas Eve, while it is still open, and reheat the next day. Refrigerate it within two hours, then reheat slices in the oven, a skillet or the microwave, whichever you prefer. US food-safety guidance is to eat cooked leftovers within three to four days.

What a Christmas Eve order costs

Here is what three common orders came to at the menu prices we checked at a Domino’s in Columbus, Ohio, on October 25, 2026. They are before tax and any fees, and your store’s prices may differ.

ForThe orderMenu total
2–3 people1 large specialty pizza, 16 Bread Bites$25.98
4–5 people2 large specialty pizzas, 16 Bread Bites, 2-liter soda$50.46
8 people3 large specialty pizzas, 2 orders of Bread Bites, 2 × 2-liter soda, Lava Cake Flight$90.92

Swap specialty pizzas ($19.99) for large cheese ($13.99) and each pizza costs $6 less. Planning on three slices per adult when pizza is the whole meal, three large pizzas give eight people 24 slices. For bigger gatherings, our group ordering guide works through the numbers, and the menu page lists the prices we checked.

Other options on the day

If you only find out on the day, try the next-nearest Domino’s for carryout — being outside its delivery area does not stop you collecting. After that, search for independent pizzerias and restaurants near you and call before driving, since Christmas hours are just as uneven elsewhere. Other pizza chains are also largely franchised, so the same advice applies: check the specific store. It is also worth having a frozen pizza at home as insurance, bought before the 24th, as many supermarkets close or shorten hours for the holiday.

Sources: CBS News, updated December 2025; Newsweek; Good Housekeeping via AOL, December 2022. We are not affiliated with Domino’s and cannot confirm any store’s hours. Spotted something out of date? Tell us.

title: Domino's Happy Hour 2026: Is There One in the US?
excerpt: Does Domino's have a happy hour? We found no US chain-wide offer. How to check your own store, and the deals that save more at any hour.
author: maha-iqbal
imageAlt: A pizza on a wooden board beside a piggy bank, coins and a calculator, with the title Domino's Happy Hour
keywords: does dominos have a happy hour

faqs.question: Does Domino’s have a happy hour?
faqs.answer: We could not find a chain-wide Domino’s happy hour in the US as of November 5, 2026. Individual stores have their own coupons, so a local offer is possible. Enter your address on dominos.com or in the app to see what your store offers.

faqs.question: What time is Domino’s happy hour?
faqs.answer: There is no national US time we can confirm. Domino’s Spain has promoted a Happy Hour from 16:30 to 18:30, and offers from 3 to 5pm or before 5pm have run in New Zealand and at selected stores in Australia, which is likely why those times come up in searches. They do not apply to US stores.

faqs.question: Does Domino’s have a 3 to 5pm deal in the US?
faqs.answer: We found no current national 3 to 5pm deal in the US. If your store runs one, it will appear in that store’s coupons, or the staff can tell you if you call.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest time to order from Domino’s?
faqs.answer: As far as we can find, price does not depend on the time of day. Choosing carryout and ordering online matters far more. The reported $7.99 large 1-topping carryout deal saved at least $6.00 against the menu prices we checked.

faqs.question: Can I use Domino’s deals at any time of day?
faqs.answer: The current Mix & Match and carryout offers are not reported with a time limit, so they should work whenever your store is taking orders. Local coupons can have their own terms, so read them before you order.

faqs.question: What is the best Domino’s deal right now?
faqs.answer: For one large pizza, the reported $7.99 carryout deal gives the biggest saving we calculated. For two people wanting variety, Mix & Match at $6.99 per item works well, and the $19.99 Perfect Combo suits a family of about five. Availability varies by store.

faqs.question: Does Domino’s Mix & Match work for delivery?
faqs.answer: It is reported to work for both delivery and carryout at participating stores, and the price can be higher at some locations. Delivery also adds a fee and a tip, so your total will be higher even at the same item price. Your store’s page has the final answer.

faqs.question: Is the $7.99 Domino’s deal available for delivery?
faqs.answer: No. Domino’s fine print describes it as carryout only and says you must ask for the offer. Prices and participation vary, and some listings show a higher price, so confirm it on your store’s page before you order.

content:
Quick answer

We could not find a Domino’s happy hour in the US. There is no chain-wide discount window we can point to, at 3–5pm or any other time. The offers that save the most, such as the $7.99 carryout deal and $6.99 Mix & Match, are not reported as limited to certain hours. Domino’s has run happy hours abroad, including in Spain, but those do not apply to US stores.

Checked November 5, 2026. Each store has its own coupons, and we cannot see them all, so a local afternoon offer is possible. The steps below show how to check yours.

If you searched for Domino’s happy hours, you were probably hoping for a simple answer like “half price from 3 to 5.” Some pages will give you one, but we could not trace any such schedule to a current US offer. What you can do is order the right way at any hour. This guide covers where the happy hour idea comes from, how to check your own store, and which deal to use for your order, with the savings worked out from real menu prices.

Does Domino’s have a happy hour?

Not as a national US offer, as far as we can find. Domino’s deals page promotes Mix & Match and a weeklong carryout offer, and two regularly updated deal roundups, from The Krazy Coupon Lady (updated November 1, 2026) and EatDrinkDeals (October 9, 2026), list nothing tied to a time of day.

The idea did not come from nowhere, though. Domino’s businesses in other countries have run real time-limited offers, and those pages turn up when you search:

How to check your store for a happy hour deal

Most US Domino’s stores are franchise-owned, and deals can differ by location. This takes about two minutes:

  1. Enter your address. Go to dominos.com or open the app and enter your address, so you see the store that actually serves you. Here is why that may not be the nearest one.
  2. Open that store’s coupons. Look for any wording about times or days, such as “before 5pm” or “Monday to Thursday.” Local offers are where a time limit would show up.
  3. Switch between carryout and delivery. Some deals only appear for one of them, so check both before deciding your store has nothing.
  4. Call if you want to be sure. Ask: “Do you run any afternoon or late-night specials, and can I get them online?” Staff can tell you about anything that is not obvious on the page.

Saw a “happy hour” code on a coupon site? Do not rely on it until it applies at checkout. Add the items to your basket and see the discount in your total before paying.

What actually changes your price, if not the time

Without a happy hour, the clock is not what moves your total. These four things are:

  • Carryout or delivery. The biggest saving here comes from a carryout-only deal, and delivery adds a fee and a tip on top.
  • How you order. Domino’s fine print says you must ask for the carryout offer, while EatDrinkDeals reports that phone orders no longer qualify. The safest route is to choose the deal in the app or on the site, and to check that your total drops before you pay.
  • Your toppings. The deal covers one topping. Each extra one usually adds $1.50 to $2, according to EatDrinkDeals, which can quietly erase part of your saving.
  • Limited-time sales. Bigger discounts come and go. EatDrinkDeals reported a 50% off pizza promotion that ran through October 11, 2026, and The Krazy Coupon Lady says $9.99 pizzas with any crust and toppings appear a few times a year. These last for days, not hours, so if you are not in a hurry they are worth waiting for.

Do not forget Domino’s Rewards

The Krazy Coupon Lady reports that members earn 10 points on each order of $5 or more (other reports say this is limited to once a day), and that 60 points can be redeemed for a free medium 2-topping pizza, among other rewards. That is a free pizza roughly every six orders, and unlike a happy hour, it works whenever you order. Our rewards guide shows how to get the most from it. Point rules can change, so check the current terms in the app.

The best time to order, if you still want to plan

Time of day will not lower your price, as far as we can find, but it can get your food to you sooner. Orders placed before the dinner rush tend to meet a quieter kitchen, while Friday and Saturday evenings and big game nights tend to be busier. Late at night, remember that the posted closing time is not your deadline, because some stores stop delivery a little earlier.
